Abstract:
Powder bed fusion (PBF) is an additive manufacturing (AM) technique that holds a great promise for alumina ceramic materials to be processed in a one step. To ensure an effective outcome, the powder material should be thoroughly tailored, and the process parameters should be appropriately investigated. These process parameters include laser power, scanning speed, hatching space, and scanning strategies. The alumina powder has been tailored and modified to be appropriately used for PBF using the spray-drying technique, and the process parameters have been predicted and selected using a developed numerical model. Different scanning speeds of 100, 200, 300, and 400 mm/s have been considered, and the other parameters have been numerically predicted. The results demonstrated that spray drying is an effective technique for tailoring the characteristics of alumina powder, such as particle shape, particle size distribution, flowability, and absorptivity, making it ideally suited for PBF processing. Furthermore, the developed numerical model demonstrated outstanding reliability in predicting the most effective laser power and hatching space for different scanning speeds, resulting in significant cost and time savings when compared to relying solely on experimental trials. Employing a scanning speed of 400 mm/s yielded a significant improvement in relative density and quality of the printed samples surpassing other scanning speeds. Moreover, this speed effectively addressed various challenges encountered by other scanning speeds. Following the optimization of process parameters, it was determined that a relative density of 94.5% could be achieved by utilizing a scanning speed of 400 mm/s, a laser power of 210 W, and a hatching space of 30 µm. However, the evaluation of mechanical performance revealed that while the microhardness of the printed alumina samples matched the values reported in the literature, the attained compressive strength fell significantly below the values reported in the literature.

Abstract:
Gas-atomized Ni-based powder tends to agglomerate, directly impacting the spreadability of printing process. In this paper, three technical methods are applied to restore the powder flowability, including regulating particle size distribution, lubricant modification, and heating treatment. As particle size increases, powder regains flowability. However, the average particle size of GH3536 powders with flowability is greater than 46 μm, which cannot meet the demand for 3D printing (15-53 μm). The flowability of GH3536 powder can be restored by adding zinc stearate lubricant. After lubricant modification, the printed samples display a 16% increase in elongation, along with a little improvement in tensile strength. This paper also investigates the flow properties change of raw powder heated at 100°C, 200°C, 300°C, and 400°C. When the temperature rises beyond 400°C, powder flowability fully returns, along with oxygen content increasing. Overall, the lubricant modification technique is appropriate in actual manufacturing, but the flow rate value of powders is typically high, exceeding 70 s/50 g. Increasing particle size and heat treatment can improve powder flowability and the flow rate of powder is less than 20 s/50 g.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34'.

Ying-Jie Li. Additive manufacturing of 6061 and 7075 aluminium alloy with selective laser melting. Unknown journal, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.70675/5f083431z1407z40f1z83bfz19a675dc42f6, doi:10.70675/5f083431z1407z40f1z83bfz19a675dc42f6.

The excerpt identifies 500°C bed preheating as sufficient for producing crack-free pure Al6061 by LPBF, with reported tensile yield strength, ultimate strength, and elongation of 60 MPa, 130 MPa, and 15%, respectively. For Al7075, a 200°C base-plate preheat did not eliminate cracking, despite producing samples with high relative density. The text groups 2xxx alloys (including Al2024), 6xxx alloys (including Al6061), and 7xxx alloys (including Al7075) as susceptible to hot cracking. For 2xxx alloys, thermal cracking was reduced by increasing laser power and reducing scanning speed, but cracks persisted even with substrate preheating from 200–400°C; therefore, the excerpt does not establish a successful crack-free temperature for Al2024 or the broader 2xxx family. It also does not provide specific preheat temperatures for all 6xxx or 7xxx alloys beyond the Al6061 and Al7075 examples. Regarding grain refiners, the excerpt gives evidence only for TiB2: increasing TiB2 from 1% to 5% refined AlSi10Mg grains from 6.32 to 1.55 μm, promoted columnar-to-equiaxed transformation, and 2 wt% produced approximately 127 HV microhardness and 444 MPa tensile strength. No information is provided here on Zr, Sc, or TiC alternatives.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'dixit2022laseradditivemanufacturing pages 16-18'.

Som Dixit and Shunyu Liu. Laser additive manufacturing of high-strength aluminum alloys: challenges and strategies. Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 6:156, Dec 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmmp6060156, doi:10.3390/jmmp6060156. This article has 100 citations.

The excerpt provides one explicit preheating condition: for LPBF/AM AA6061, adding 1 wt.% Zr together with a heated build plate at 100 °C significantly reduced porosity and cracking. It does not state the preheat temperatures required for crack-free processing of AA7075, AA2024, generic 2xxx, 6xxx, or 7xxx alloys, nor does it identify failed preheat temperatures. Those values would need to be obtained from other portions of the article or its cited studies. The excerpt emphasizes that alloy modification can serve as an alternative or complement to preheating. Si reduces cracking through lower melting/solidification ranges, improved liquid feeding, lower thermal expansion, reduced cooling-related thermal stress, and grain refinement. Ti promotes Al3Ti-based heterogeneous nucleation and columnar-to-equiaxed transition; approximately 1.5 wt.% Ti is reported as an optimum for grain refinement without excessive brittleness. TiC, TiN, and TiB2 particles can improve strength and solidification behavior, while combined Ti/TiN additions improve wettability and reduce ceramic-particle agglomeration. Although the question specifically asks about Zr and Sc, this excerpt only explicitly reports the 1 wt.% Zr/100 °C AA6061 case; it does not provide Sc-specific processing temperatures or crack-failure thresholds.

It specifically reports that adding 3–4 wt% Si improves Al7075 processability and alleviates cracking by promoting eutectic phases, reducing melting temperature and the solidification range, and improving late-stage melt flow. TiB2 is mentioned only as part of a combination of 4 wt% Si and 2 wt% TiB2 in an Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloy; the excerpt does not provide isolated TiB2 results or discuss Zr, Sc, or TiC. Therefore, the requested comparison of Zr, Sc, TiB2, and TiC versus preheating cannot be completed from this excerpt alone.

For CM247LC and IN713LC, preheating up to approximately 900 °C did not eliminate hot cracking; cracks remained associated with γ’ precipitation and segregation of carbide-forming elements at cell boundaries. The study indicates that preheating above the γ’-solvus temperature—reported as exceeding 1200 °C—can produce sufficiently slower cooling rates to fully suppress cracks in the investigated alloys. The introduction mentions IN738 among γ’-strengthened Ni-based superalloys and cites prior work on its cracking susceptibility, including solidification cracking linked to segregation and low-melting γ/γ’ eutectic formation, but this excerpt does not provide an IN738LC preheat temperature or a temperature that eliminated cracking. It also provides no preheat data for Rene 80 or for the requested non-nickel alloy families. Therefore, the only explicit crack-elimination temperature range supported here is above 1200 °C for CM247LC and IN713LC under the study’s investigated conditions.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 7-9'.

Sina Rezaei, Sara Biamino, Federica Bondioli, Daniele Ugues, Paolo Fino, and Mariangela Lombardi. Powder degradation and recycling strategies for aluminum alloys in additive manufacturing: a comprehensive review. Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app16136822, doi:10.3390/app16136822. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt directly supports the concern that elevated thermal exposure during LPBF can degrade powder through partial sintering, satelliting, and agglomeration. Particles near the melt pool or exposed to local overheating may form solid necks or fuse into larger clusters. These agglomerates behave as oversized, irregular powder, shifting the particle-size distribution toward coarser sizes and reducing the volume of free-flowing, reusable material. The resulting degradation can impair flow through recoaters or nozzles, disturb powder spreading, and create streaks or local powder-bed irregularities. Agglomerates may also be retained during sieving, causing material loss, or obstruct powder-delivery systems. Because larger clusters require more energy to melt completely, they may produce inclusions or lack-of-fusion defects when standard parameters are optimized for individual particles. The excerpt further associates uncontrolled sintering with reduced flowability, increased porosity, poor surface finish, and dimensional inaccuracies. It notes that thermal exposure can also increase particle surface roughness and alter thermal absorption, potentially contributing to incomplete melting and local lack-of-fusion defects. However, this passage does not specifically quantify the effects of 400–600°C preheating or address oxidation/nitridation of aluminum or titanium, magnesium/zinc evaporation, oxygen-control requirements, diffusion bonding to the build plate, or build-plate thermal distortion.

The excerpt directly addresses several process complications associated with elevated platform temperatures in LPBF of nickel aluminum bronze, particularly in the 400–550 °C range. The heated-platform window was selected using CALPHAD predictions to promote desirable phases while mitigating brittle-phase formation, indicating that high-temperature processing can alter phase stability and increase brittleness if poorly controlled. The study explicitly reports that process temperature strongly influences distortion and cracking, making thermal-mechanical defects a central concern during hot builds. It evaluated platform temperatures from 25 °C to 550 °C and used crack and distortion measurements to identify suitable conditions. The excerpt does not provide evidence about powder sintering, caking, agglomeration, flowability degradation, aluminum or titanium oxidation/nitridation, magnesium or zinc evaporation, powder degradation, diffusion bonding to the build plate, or build-plate distortion specifically. However, it emphasizes the importance of atmospheric control: the EOS M290-HT maintains oxygen concentrations below 200 ppm using gas purification, because low oxygen helps ensure material quality and minimize defects. The machine also uses active heating and infrared monitoring to maintain temperature uniformity, since temperature gradients can contribute to distortion, residual stress, and cracking.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'raza2022powderdegradationduring pages 30-33'.

A Raza. Powder degradation during powder bed fusion processing: impact of processing conditions and alloy composition. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt does not directly evaluate 400–600°C LPBF preheating, powder sintering or caking, magnesium/zinc evaporation, diffusion bonding to the build plate, or build-plate thermal distortion. It does provide relevant context for powder degradation during LPBF. Conventional PBF-LB is described as operating with the powder bed near ambient temperature in an inert environment, which limits further atmospheric oxidation after passive oxide layers form. Consequently, atmospheric oxidation is considered less important than spatter accumulation for reused powder. Spatters can be hot, partly molten particles that are especially prone to oxidation when exposed to oxygen in the build chamber. Their accumulation can alter powder particle-size distribution, morphology, and flowability, and can increase the powder bed’s oxygen concentration. This may promote oxide inclusions in manufactured parts and cause local variations in energy absorption. The excerpt also notes that spatter generation depends on beam energy and size, scan speed, material, and processing-gas purity. Therefore, elevated-temperature builds could plausibly intensify oxidation-related and powder-flow concerns identified here, but the excerpt itself does not establish specific effects of 400–600°C preheating, including sintering/agglomeration thresholds, nitridation, volatile-element loss, oxygen limits, part-to-plate bonding, or thermal distortion.

The excerpt provides direct evidence on LPBF build-plate compatibility, adhesion, dilution, and interfacial failure, although it concerns molybdenum printed on AISI 304 rather than aluminum printed on steel, titanium, or copper. Printing Mo on an AISI 304 plate initially failed because of poor adhesion: delamination began after approximately 10 layers and ultimately caused recoater collision. Interface analysis found that the principal crack originated where Mo dilution was approximately 40–50 wt.%. The diluted Mo–Fe–Cr–Ni region contained brittle Sigma phase, which was identified by XRD and extraction; this phase, together with LPBF residual stresses, was considered a preferential path for crack propagation and brittle fracture. Cracks also followed Mo-enriched regions and occurred near approximately 45 wt.% Mo. In contrast, an oxygen-free electronic copper (Cu OFE/Cu C2) plate showed good compatibility with Mo, and printing remained stable throughout production. A modified AISI 304 platform with grooves, cavities, vacuum retention, and a 2 mm Mo sheet also enabled successful printing while reducing the need for a full Mo build plate. Abstract:
Compared to conventional fabrication methods, additive manufacturing (AM) introduces new opportunities in terms of design freedom and part complexity due to the incremental layer‐by‐layer process. For tooling applications, higher cutting speeds can be realized by implementing of internal cooling channels in tools that could not be fabricated otherwise. However, processability of high‐alloyed tool steels with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) faces certain restrictions. In addition to pore formation, severe cracking caused by a combination of process‐related stresses due to the high thermal gradient and susceptible materials may occur. This work aims to clarify the occurrence of process‐related defects in dependence of the applied energy input of a high‐alloyed cold‐work tool steel and to correlate it to the evolution of microstructure respectively solidification structure. Defect surfaces and structural evolution are investigated. The results exhibit that with increasing energy input porosity changes from lack‐of‐fusion to keyhole porosity. Most recently published investigations suggest cold cracking as predominant failure mechanism during LPBF of tool steels. However, for the investigated material, the present study clearly reveals that, irrespective of the chosen energy input, hot cracks are formed. Crack propagation can be connected to the solidification structure and possible thermal stress accumulations caused by the process.

Abstract:
Hot working tool steels (HWTS) are popular for industrial applications such as injection molding tools, and casting dies because of their high wear resistance, fatigue, strength, and toughness properties, even at elevated temperatures. Conventionally, they go through multi-stage heat treatments in order to attain targeted microstructures. Achieving such microstructures with a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process will require tailor-made process parameters since it is characterized by non-equilibrium conditions, non-uniform temperature distribution, and metastable phase formation. Recent advances in the LPBF qualification of 1.2343/4 HWTS have shown commendable results but are still fraught with the limitations of poor ductility or extra post-heat treatment steps. For the industrial competitiveness of LPBF HWTS, the enhancement of strength and ductility and elimination of post processing is critical. Therefore, minimizing retained austenite in the as-built samples through pre-heat treatment or alloying to reduce post heat treatments without sacrificing strength will be economically important for industry. In this work, 1.2343 HWTS and its modified form were LPBF printed both in the as-built, pre- and post-heat-treated conditions. The results are discussed based on the correlations of the powder properties with LPBF—part density, microstructure, and mechanical properties.

Abstract:
The ability to manufacture complex designs from multiple materials has long been a key objective for applications operating in extreme environments. Multi-material (MM) additive manufacturing (MMAM) has significantly enhanced the functionality of additive manufacturing (AM) by enabling the integration of dissimilar alloys while leveraging the inherent advantages of AM, including design flexibility, reduced material waste, and rapid production, with the ability to tailor mechanical properties through spatial material distribution and local processing conditions. This process unlocks unprecedented opportunities across industries such as aerospace, automotive, biomedical, energy, and nuclear sectors. This article provides a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art in MMAM, focusing on the manufacturing processes, molten pool formation, alloy compatibility, and bimetallic interface characteristics—including microstructural and mechanical properties—as well as modeling and simulation approaches for performance prediction and optimization, with developments tracked from 2013 to 2024. This review article predominantly focuses on: (i) MM-laser powder bed fusion, (ii) MM-directed energy deposition, and (iii) MM-wire-arc AM by detailing the mechanisms of molten pool formation at the interface and dissimilar alloy material compatibilities. Subsequently, the article provides an in-depth analysis of the meso- and micro-structural characteristics at the interface in bimetallic structures across widely employed MMAM alloys. The mechanics of MMs under various mechanical properties are presented, including microhardness/micro-indentation, tensile, flexural, compression, and fatigue strength, which are critical for MMAM applications in extreme conditions. In addition, current modeling and simulation approaches for MMAM are discussed with respect to the challenges and opportunities to increase MMAM adoption. The article concludes with a future roadmap for advancing MMAM by overcoming feedstock and build material cross-contamination, monitoring the in situ process, standardizing MM testing, and further developing thermo-mechanical modeling, specifically, for MMAM.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to provide the latest powder deposition approaches in multimaterial laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and to discuss the produced interface properties based on effects caused by the intrinsic material compatibility, process parameters, powder characteristics, melt pool dynamics, and thermal models. It reviews the current metallurgical challenges at the diffusion zone of the pairs, including the formation of brittle intermetallic phases and other microstructural and thermodynamical challenges to provide better solutions to tackle these problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review paper used a systematic approach to search for and investigate notable works and peer-reviewed publications concerning multimaterial LPBF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The key results explain how the interface type and dynamic process parameter optimization for different layers at the interface, near the interface, and within single materials affect the avoidance of energy-related defects. Understanding the differences in intrinsic material properties such as thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, and melting point, allows us to initially select the most appropriate interface type. The effects of process parameters and powder characteristics are discussed. Common challenges, including microstructural defects, melt-pool-induced defects, and unwanted brittle intermetallic phases, can be solved by nonequilibrium phase diagram simulations, proper interface-type selection, better alloy design, and the use of interlayers at the interface.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By outlining the powder deposition approaches and their interface properties and challenges in multimaterial LPBF, this study provides deeper metallurgical aspects shared among material pairs. This helps researchers in troubleshooting common interface challenges based on the guidelines suggested in this paper.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adem.202000833, doi:10.1002/adem.202000833. This article has 48 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports the conclusion that preheating affects LPBF cracking through both thermal-gradient reduction and suppression of martensitic transformation. For H13 hot-work tool steel, preheating up to 200 °C was associated with compressive stresses, while 300–400 °C produced tensile stresses because the temperature exceeded the martensite-start temperature. Separate cited work reported reduced crack density in H13 with elevated-temperature preheating, and crack density in X65MoCrWV3-2 was reduced with preheating up to 300 °C. For high-speed steel M3:2 (HS 6-5-3, containing 1.20 wt% carbon), a strong decrease in crack density was observed at 300 °C. The text does not establish that 200, 400, or 500 °C universally produces crack-free parts, nor does it provide direct results for M2, M50, or HS6-5-3-8 specifically. It explains that conventional high-carbon tool steels form hard, low-ductility carbon martensite during rapid cooling, making them susceptible to cracking; preheating above the martensite-start temperature can suppress this transformation. However, the excerpt alone cannot determine an optimum or crack-free temperature at 500 °C.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a layerwise production process that creates three-dimensional objects according to a digital model. This technology has demonstrated to be a promising alternative to conventional manufacturing methods for various industrial sectors, such as aerospace, automotive, biomedical, and energy. AM offers several advantages, like design flexibility, material efficiency, functional integration, and rapid prototyping. As regards metal parts, conventional AM techniques using infrared laser sources face some limitations in processing high-reflectivity and high-conductivity materials or alloys, such as aluminum, copper, gold, and silver. These materials have low absorption of infrared radiation, which results in unstable and shallow melt pools, poor surface quality, and high porosity. To overcome these challenges, green and blue laser sources have been proposed for AM processes. This review provides an overview of the recent developments and applications of green and blue laser sources for powder bed fusion of copper and its alloys, focusing on the effects of process parameters on the melt pool dynamics, microstructure formation, and thermal and electrical properties of the fabricated parts. This review also presents the main applications of AM of copper and its alloys together with potential opportunities for future developments.

Abstract:
This study investigates the physicochemical and toxicological properties of Scalmalloy powder emissions generated during Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF), focusing on the impact of particle morphology, oxidation, and size distribution on biological responses. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) analyses revealed significant variations in particle characteristics, with the highest oxidation levels and irregular morphologies observed in exhaust-derived powders. In vitro cytotoxicity evaluations using A549 lung epithelial cells showed significant reductions in cell viability (~60 to 69%) and increased oxidative stress (p < 0.05) upon exposure to virgin sieved (<20 µm) and exhaust powder samples. Conversely, samples from the build plate, overflow, and dispenser exhibited high cell viability (>85%). Indirect exposure through media incubation resulted in minimal cytotoxicity, suggesting that metal dissolution plays a limited role in toxicity under the studied conditions. The findings highlight the influence of particle morphology and oxidation on cytotoxic responses and underscore the need for controlled powder handling to mitigate occupational exposure risks in LPBF environments.

Abstract:

 Lightweight design is very closely associated with additive manufacturing. Besides the design possibilities offered by this technology, the material used also plays a key role. Especially in the LPBF process, the production of the powder and the processing of the material is a major challenge. This applies in particular to magnesium alloys as a lightweight material. Due to its low density and good strength and rigidity properties, this material is ideal for lightweight engineering applications. The basis of this contribution is a risk assessment (including a detailed FMEA and measures to minimize risks) for the processing and handling of magnesium powder in the LPBF process. As part of the practical tests, several test specimens with existing parameters for AZ91D were printed, and their properties (relative density, microstructure and bonding behaviour) were analysed. By adjusting the alloy composition (improved evaporation characteristics) and optimizing the process (e.g. optimum inert gas flow, platform temperature) and the process parameters, it is possible to process magnesium more economically in the LPBF process.

Abstract:
Magnesium-based alloy WE43 is a state-of-the-art bioresorbable metallic implant material. There is a need for implants with both complex geometries to match the mechanical properties of bone and refined microstructure for controlled resorption. Additive manufacturing (AM) using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) presents a viable fabrication method for implant applications, as it offers near-net-shape geometrical control, allows for geometry customization based on an individual patient, and fast cooling rates to achieve a refined microstructure. In this study, the laser–alloy interaction is investigated over a range of LPBF-relevant processing conditions to reveal melt-pool dynamics, pore formation, and the microstructure of laser-melted WE43. In situ X-ray imaging reveals distinct laser-induced vapor depression morphology regimes, with minimal pore formation at laser-scan speeds greater than 500 mm/s. Optical and electron microscopy of cross-sectioned laser tracks reveal three distinct microstructural regimes that can be controlled by adjusting laser-scan parameters: columnar, dendritic, and banded microstructures. These regimes are consistent with those predicted by the analytic solidification theory for conduction-mode welding, but not for keyhole-mode tracks. The results provide insight into the fundamental laser–material interactions of the WE43 alloy under AM-processing conditions and are critical for the successful implementation of LPBF-produced WE43 parts in biomedical applications.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of Zn-based metals exhibits prominent advantages to produce customized biodegradable implants. However, massive evaporation occurs during laser melting of Zn so that it becomes a critical issue to modulate laser energy input and gas shielding conditions to eliminate the negative effect of evaporation fume during the LPBF process. In this research, two numerical models were established to simulate the interaction between the scanning laser and Zn metal as well as the interaction between the shielding gas flow and the evaporation fume, respectively. The first model predicted the evaporation rate under different laser energy input by taking the effect of evaporation on the conservation of energy, momentum, and mass into consideration. With the evaporation rate as the input, the second model predicted the elimination effect of evaporation fume under different conditions of shielding gas flow by taking the effect of the gas circulation system including geometrical design and flow rate. In the case involving an adequate laser energy input and an optimized shielding gas flow, the evaporation fume was efficiently removed from the processing chamber during the LPBF process. Furthermore, the influence of evaporation on surface quality densification was discussed by comparing LPBF of pure Zn and a Titanium alloy. The established numerical analysis not only helps to find the adequate laser energy input and the optimized shielding gas flow for the LPBF of Zn based metal, but is also beneficial to understand the influence of evaporation on the LPBF process.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'fields2024structuralandcompositional pages 58-63'.

B Fields. Structural and compositional control of steel and aluminum alloys via laser powder bed fusion processing. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt directly addresses evaporative loss of Mg and Zn during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of a 7xxx aluminum alloy. Because Zn and Mg have substantially lower boiling points (907°C and 1091°C) than Al and Cu (2470°C and 2562°C), selective evaporation is expected when the melt pool reaches elevated temperatures. Across the tested process-parameter range, increasing volumetric energy density reduced the concentrations of both elements in the printed material. Zn was lost preferentially relative to Mg, causing the Zn:Mg ratio to decrease by as much as 33% compared with the starting powder. The authors report that energy density, rather than laser power alone, is a useful predictor of elemental evaporation. They model evaporation using vapor pressures and vaporization fluxes through the Langmuir equation, while melt-pool geometry is estimated with the Rosenthal equation; the model and experiments show a strong initial increase in evaporation that levels off at higher energy densities. The excerpt does not provide quantitative data on chamber condensate, fume, soot, or redeposition, nor does it specify required oxygen concentration (ppm O2), oxygen-control limits, or dew-point requirements for LPBF aluminum processing. It also does not report evaporation directly from loose powder separately from melt-pool evaporation.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 11-12'.

Javid Hussain, Abdul Wahid Shah, Jabir Ali Siddique, and Shou-Jin Sun. Metallurgical aspects of additively manufactured aluminum alloys: a review. Metals and Materials International, Oct 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12540-026-02247-z, doi:10.1007/s12540-026-02247-z. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies Mg and Zn evaporation as important problems in laser processing of aluminum alloys. Aluminum’s low laser absorption and high reflectivity require relatively high laser power, which can overheat the melt pool and vaporize low-boiling-point Mg and Zn. Reported evaporation rates vary substantially because they depend on laser power, scan speed, atmosphere control, and measurement methods. The text also notes that Mg and Zn losses are common at high energy densities or powder feed rates, although scan speed effects are inconsistent; evaporation is governed by melt-pool temperature, recoil pressure, and vapor-plume dynamics rather than volumetric energy density alone. Aluminum powder oxidation is another key concern: hydrophilic powder readily forms alumina, reducing absorption and causing contamination and poor bonding. Humid powder aging increases alumina and hydroxide inclusions and raises oxygen and hydrogen content, destabilizing the melt pool. Atmosphere and powder-moisture control are therefore essential, particularly because hydrogen can cause gas porosity. However, this excerpt does not provide quantitative condensate, fume, or soot measurements, nor does it specify a required chamber oxygen concentration in ppm or a dew-point limit. It only states that atmosphere control and moisture management affect evaporation, oxidation, and defect formation.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 38-42'.

Ying-Jie Li. Additive manufacturing of 6061 and 7075 aluminium alloy with selective laser melting. Unknown journal, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.70675/5f083431z1407z40f1z83bfz19a675dc42f6, doi:10.70675/5f083431z1407z40f1z83bfz19a675dc42f6.

The excerpt directly addresses evaporative loss of alloying elements during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of aluminum alloys. Because LPBF uses high-energy-density lasers and produces high-temperature melt pools, relatively low-boiling-point elements—including magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), and copper—are susceptible to volatilization. The cited evaporation temperatures are approximately 1090°C for Mg and 907°C for Zn. Loss of these elements can create nonuniform chemical composition and substantially reduce alloy strength and toughness. This is especially important for heat-treatable alloys: Mg contributes to strengthening in 6061, including through formation of the Mg2Si phase, while Mg and Zn form the MgZn2 strengthening phase that is central to 7075 performance. The excerpt does not provide quantitative measurements of Mg/Zn mass loss, vaporization rates, condensate, fume, soot, or chamber contamination during LPBF. It also does not specify required oxygen concentration in ppm, allowable oxygen limits, inert-gas purity, or dew-point requirements for aluminum LPBF. Therefore, the passage supports the general mechanism and metallurgical consequences of Mg/Zn evaporation, but additional process or equipment literature is needed for numerical oxygen and moisture specifications and for characterization of condensed vapor products.

Nikoletta Sargioti, Leonidas Karavias, Leonidas Gargalis, Anna Karatza, Elias P. Koumoulos, and Evangelia K. Karaxi. Physicochemical and toxicological properties of particles emitted from scalmalloy during the lpbf process. Toxics, 13:398, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/toxics13050398, doi:10.3390/toxics13050398. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt directly supports the relevance of magnesium and zinc evaporation during LPBF of aluminum alloys: elevated-temperature melting can cause these alloying elements to evaporate, producing vapor plumes and condensates. The resulting evaporation-induced composition changes may generate non-equilibrium phases and localized inhomogeneities, potentially affecting component integrity. The text also discusses oxidation and oxygen accumulation in aluminum powders, especially under repeated laser exposure. It reports that, over five production cycles, AlSi10Mg powder oxygen content increased by 120 ppm when affected by laser-induced heating, compared with only a 10 ppm increase for powder that was recycled without heat exposure. Oxidized spatter can also be returned to the powder supply and increase oxygen content over successive reuse cycles. These data concern powder oxygen changes rather than a specified chamber oxygen setpoint. The excerpt does not provide a required oxygen concentration in ppm for operating an LPBF aluminum-alloy chamber, nor does it state a dew-point requirement. It also does not specifically characterize condensate, fume, or soot deposits in the chamber beyond describing vapor plumes, condensates, and oxidized spatter. Further process-engineering sources would therefore be needed for validated O2 and dew-point specifications.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'qin2021influenceoflaser pages 10-12'.

Yu Qin, Jinge Liu, Yanzhe Chen, Peng Wen, Yufeng Zheng, Yun Tian, Maximilian Voshage, and Johannes Henrich Schleifenbaum. Influence of laser energy input and shielding gas flow on evaporation fume during laser powder bed fusion of zn metal. Materials, 14:2677, May 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14102677, doi:10.3390/ma14102677. This article has 43 citations.

The excerpt provides relevant information on evaporation and fume formation during LPBF of Zn and, more generally, Zn/Mg alloys, but it does not specifically characterize aluminum alloy powder or melt-pool evaporation. It states that Zn and Mg can undergo massive evaporation losses sufficient to cause substantial compositional changes. Evaporation is promoted by increasing molten-pool temperature and laser energy input; once the vaporization point is exceeded, additional energy produces more evaporation rather than a continued substantial temperature rise, with evaporation carrying excess heat away. Metal vapor cools and condenses into nanoscale evaporation-fume particles, reported here as approximately 10–150 nm in diameter. These particles can scatter the laser beam, reduce the actual energy delivered to the powder bed, destabilize melting, increase porosity, and contaminate or potentially damage chamber optics. Insufficient shielding-gas flow allows residual fume to accumulate, whereas adequate flow removes it and maintains a clean processing atmosphere. Excessively strong flow can become turbulent and disturb powder or melt-pool behavior. The excerpt does not provide quantitative evaporative-loss rates for aluminum, Mg, or Zn, nor does it discuss soot specifically. It also gives no oxygen-concentration or dew-point requirements for LPBF of aluminum alloys; those specifications would need to be obtained from other sources.

URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14102677, doi:10.3390/ma14102677. This article has 43 citations.

This excerpt is relevant to evaporation and fume behavior, particularly for Zn and Mg, but it does not directly address aluminum-alloy LPBF oxygen ppm limits or dew-point requirements. The Langmuir-model discussion indicates that evaporation flux increases with molten-pool temperature and that greater laser energy input increases alloying-element evaporation loss. Among the listed elements, the predicted evaporation-loss tendency is Zn > Mg > Fe > Ti, suggesting that Zn is more volatile than Mg under comparable conditions. The text also notes that relative compositional loss depends on the initial concentration of an alloying element, so a low-concentration element can experience a larger relative depletion. In LPBF, the Knudsen layer limits continuous evaporation, while condensation of metal vapor can return material to the molten pool, reducing total loss compared with ideal vacuum evaporation. For Zn, measured evaporation rates increased from 0.23 mg/s at 70 W to 0.57 mg/s at 90 W. Shielding-gas simulations show that no gas flow allows fume to rise and saturate the chamber; insufficient flow removes some fume but leaves residual fume that accumulates over time. The excerpt provides no measurements or specifications for condensate, soot, oxygen concentration, or dew point in aluminum-alloy processing.

Yu Qin, Jinge Liu, Yanzhe Chen, Peng Wen, Yufeng Zheng, Yun Tian, Maximilian Voshage, and Johannes Henrich Schleifenbaum. The excerpt is relevant to the general issue of metal evaporation, condensate/fume transport, and shielding-gas management in LPBF, but it focuses on Zn rather than aluminum alloys or Mg. It states that Zn undergoes substantial evaporation during laser melting and that evaporation can generate fume requiring removal from the processing chamber. The study developed two numerical models: one predicts evaporation rate as a function of laser energy input while accounting for energy, momentum, and mass conservation; the other predicts fume removal under different shielding-gas flow rates and circulation-system geometries. Adequate laser energy input combined with optimized shielding-gas flow was reported to efficiently remove evaporation fume. The introduction also links evaporation to keyhole formation, recoil pressure, altered melt-pool temperature and flow, heat loss, porosity, and spatter. However, the provided pages contain no quantitative Mg or Zn evaporation-loss data for aluminum-alloy powder or melt pools, no characterization of condensate or soot, and no numerical oxygen concentration or dew-point requirements for LPBF of aluminum alloys. Therefore, this excerpt cannot establish the requested ppm O2 or moisture limits.

                             heater to reduce or eliminate heat loss through radiation and convection on the top surface
                             of the heater. A thermocouple 1 (T1) measured the temperature after (above) the top
                         ﬁberboard insulation. Thermocouple 2 (T2) measured the temperature below the heater
                          while thermocouple 3 (T3) measured the temperature below the bottom insulation, which

                           took 90 min.

                          320 × 315 × 20 mm stainless steel plate placed above the heater. This would provide

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Rank | Recommendation | Rationale / evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **Do not make 500 °C the default for aluminium screening.** Use Tier A (≤200 °C) for AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and reserve Tier B for unmodified 6xxx experiments, in-situ heat treatment, or exceptionally stress-sensitive geometries. | AlSi10Mg normally prints without high preheat; Scalmalloy uses about 200 °C for in-situ clustering rather than crack prevention. Unmodified 6061 has been made crack-free at 500 °C, but inoculated alloys can achieve comparable crack control at much lower temperature (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031). |
| 2 | **Prefer grain-refining chemistry over a 500 °C plate for 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx development.** Screen Zr/Sc, Ti/TiB₂, TiC, CaB₆, and eutectic-forming additions first. | Zr nanoparticles produced crack-free, fully dense 6061/7075; 1 wt% Zr with 100 °C reduced 6061 cracking; TiAl₃ prevented 6061 cracking; 1.5 wt% Ti prevented cracking in Al-Cu-Mg. By contrast, 200 °C failed for 7075 and 200–400 °C failed to eliminate 2xxx cracking (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000032). |
| 3 | **Replace the 6061 heater block with a mechanically retained steel, precipitation-resistant stainless steel, Ni alloy, or ceramic heater carrier.** Do not structurally load 6061 at 500 °C. | High-temperature platforms require all supporting and moving components to tolerate sustained heat. A ceramic resistive heater can reach the required temperature, but conductive losses through surrounding steel hardware can prevent the plate from reaching its target (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056). |
| 4 | **Thermally isolate the heater assembly from the piston and cylinder.** Use thick low-conductivity ceramic board/fibre insulation, minimized metallic contact area, slender thermal breaks, and radiation shields. | In the Aeroswift study, multiple metal contacts and only 5 mm insulation limited a nominal 600 °C system to much lower plate temperatures; the insulation was only 44% effective. Improved isolation was predicted to permit approximately 650 °C without more heater power (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056). |
| 5 | **Use a separately water-cooled piston head, seal carrier, actuator interface, and cylinder rim—but interlock cooling flow with heater power.** | Cooling protects bearings, seals, encoder/actuator components, and the honed bore while allowing the removable plate to remain hot. The strong resulting gradient makes clearance and plate bowing critical; commercial high-temperature systems likewise incorporate chamber cooling (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000042). |
| 6 | **Size the cold diametral clearance from the worst differential expansion, not the Tier-A value.** For a Ø75 mm 6061 plate at 500 °C in a 316L bore near 55 °C, differential diametral growth is approximately 0.36–0.41 mm; specify at least about 0.50–0.65 mm cold diametral clearance before adding tolerances, cylindricity, bow, deposits, and seizure margin. | Using representative mean CTEs of approximately 24–25 µm·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for 6061 and 16–17 µm·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for 316L gives about 0.18–0.21 mm **radial** closure—substantially more than the stated 0.14 mm Tier-A closure. The final fit must be validated thermally because a cooled bore and hot plate are non-isothermal. |
| 7 | **Do not use an elastomer as the hot-edge powder seal.** Use a replaceable compliant graphite felt/foil ring or aluminosilicate/other ceramic-fibre wiper outside the precision guiding land; add a stepped labyrinth and powder-catching annulus. | Elastomers are unsuitable around 500 °C, while fibrous high-temperature insulation and graphite tolerate the thermal environment. A labyrinth limits direct powder migration without requiring a zero-clearance sliding fit. Published commercial clearances and proprietary seal geometries are generally unavailable, so qualification testing is required (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000056). |
| 8 | **Decouple guidance from sealing.** Guide the piston on a cool, long lower land or separate bearing; let the upper hot plate float radially within its calculated clearance. | A hot plate tightly guided by the cooler honed bore risks seizure, galling, bore scoring, and plate buckling. The compliant upper seal should exclude powder, not carry lateral load. |
| 9 | **For aluminium builds, retain an aluminium-family sacrificial build plate whenever possible.** Start with 6061/5083 at ≤200 °C; evaluate 4032 or another qualified high-Si wrought/cast plate for Tier B. | Like-on-like aluminium gives predictable remelting, wetting, and removal. Higher-Si aluminium offers lower CTE and better elevated-temperature dimensional stability than 6061, but its LPBF interface, brittleness, flatness, and machinability must be tested. Evidence for specific 4032/A390 LPBF substrate qualification is sparse, so treat this as an engineering trial rather than a literature-proven substitution. |
| 10 | **Use hypereutectic Al-Si or Al-SiC only after coupon-level interface qualification; do not make ceramic-rich Al-SiC the first Tier-B plate.** | Controlled-expansion Al-Si and Al-SiC can reduce clearance closure, but reduced ductility, heterogeneous remelting, ceramic exposure, thermal fatigue, machining difficulty, and uncertain first-layer bonding can outweigh the CTE benefit. Compositionally compatible metallic Al-Si is the lower-risk first trial. |
| 11 | **Avoid direct aluminium deposition on steel or Invar unless a deliberately engineered interlayer/interface is acceptable.** Use a removable aluminium insert clamped to a steel heater carrier instead. | Dissimilar LPBF interfaces can form brittle intermetallics, crack, or delaminate because of incompatible melting points, conductivities, and CTEs. Mo on stainless steel, for example, delaminated after roughly ten layers where a brittle diluted phase formed, demonstrating that substrate compatibility can dominate the build (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| 12 | **Use alloy-matched substrates by material family:** aluminium plate for Al, steel plate for steels, Ni-alloy plate for Ni superalloys, Ti plate for Ti alloys, and compatible Cu/Cu-alloy plate for copper. | Matched plates minimize brittle dilution zones and differential contraction. Where matching is impractical, use a replaceable sheet/interlayer: a retained Mo sheet or Cu-OFE substrate solved an otherwise unsuccessful Mo/stainless interface in published work (pqac-00000020). |
| 13 | **Control oxygen to below 200 ppm at minimum and preferably below 100 ppm before heating; target still lower values for Ti, Mg-rich Al, and long hot soaks. Measure moisture/dew point independently.** | Reported high-temperature systems operate below 200 ppm; Aconity work reports below 100 ppm. Aluminium powder exposed to laser heating gained about 120 ppm oxygen over five cycles versus 10 ppm without heat exposure, and hot spatter is especially oxidation-prone (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000057). |
| 14 | **Bake/purge the empty chamber and hot-zone hardware before admitting production powder, and use only high-temperature-compatible seals, wiring, insulation, and lubricants.** | Heating releases adsorbed water from chamber walls, oxide/hydroxide-bearing powder, insulation, and seals. Moisture thickens aluminium oxide/hydroxide films, impairs spreading and bonding, and supplies hydrogen that can create porosity (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). |
| 15 | **Provide uniform, controllable cross-flow plus an accessible condensate trap upstream of the filter and optics.** Characterize flow at hot operating conditions. | Mg and Zn boil at approximately 1091 and 907 °C and are selectively lost from Al melt pools; condensed metal/oxide particles can be approximately 10–150 nm, scatter the laser, contaminate optics, and accumulate if gas flow is inadequate. Excessive or turbulent flow can disturb powder, so simply increasing flow is not sufficient (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039). |
| 16 | **Thermally shield and, where needed, actively cool the laser window, O₂ sensor sampling line, recoater drive, hopper throat, camera, and chamber lid.** Locate the O₂ sensor in a conditioned bypass rather than directly above the hot bed. | A 500 °C plate radiates strongly into a 6 L chamber; commercial high-temperature systems incorporate chamber cooling and active monitoring. Fume and condensate additionally threaten the window and sensor, while temperature shifts can bias sensors and expand recoater hardware (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042). |
| 17 | **Use a thermally robust recoater and qualify hot spreading with the actual powder.** Prefer a replaceable metal/ceramic blade, force monitoring, and powder with tightly controlled fines; minimize particles below roughly 15 µm for Tier-B trials. | Fines, moisture, oxide coatings, agglomerates, and partial sintering increase cohesion and produce streaks or low-density layers. Agglomerates can obstruct delivery, be dragged by the blade, and create lack-of-fusion defects; heat-affected aluminium condensate further reduces flowability (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). |
| 18 | **Limit and log each powder lot’s cumulative hot exposure.** Initially restrict 500 °C trials to short, shallow builds; segregate hot-zone powder, sieve it, and test oxygen, PSD, flow/spread density, and Mg/Zn composition before reuse. | Thermal exposure produces necking, satellites, agglomeration and oxide/hydroxide condensate. Heat-affected aluminium powder showed much greater oxygen pickup, while agglomerates shift PSD, reduce reusable yield and impair recoating (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000049). |
| 19 | **Design the first layers and removal process for stronger plate bonding at 400–500 °C.** Include sacrificial interface stock, reduced first-layer energy where validated, EDM/bandsaw access, and a plate resurfacing allowance. | Reduced thermal gradients improve bonding and reduce delamination, but also reduce contraction-assisted release and can enlarge the metallurgically mixed interface. Dissimilar interfaces may instead form brittle phases, so mechanical keys or interlayers should be deliberate, not accidental (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| 20 | **Instrument temperature at the plate top, heater, piston head, bore, gas outlet, lid/window and sensor bay; independently trip on overtemperature, lost cooling, low flow, or rising O₂. Consider VCSEL/laser-diode top-layer heating only as a later uniformity upgrade.** | A heater thermocouple can substantially overstate plate temperature: one ceramic-heater design predicted 395 °C at the heater but only 374 °C at the substrate. EOS-type VCSEL heating plus IR feedback can homogenize each recoated layer rapidly, while laser-diode heating has demonstrated in-situ annealing; these methods add optical and control complexity but address the decay of baseplate heating with build height (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046). |


*Table: Prioritized engineering recommendations for a 500 °C LPBF tier, including thermal architecture, atmosphere, powder handling, substrate selection, sealing, and the plate-to-bore fit.*

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.

max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence

List of target names to search for.
Usage:

target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

List of drug names to generate or filter results.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
