## Build-Plate Preheating in Laser Powder Bed Fusion: When Is 400–600 °C Needed, What Complications Arise, and How Should the Platform Be Designed?

This review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature on high-temperature build-plate preheating for LPBF, covering preheat requirements by alloy class, practical complications, commercial machine implementations, build-plate materials, and plate-to-bore sealing strategies. The findings are organized around the three questions posed, followed by the requested summary table and ranked design recommendations.

---

### 1. When Is 400–600 °C Preheat Actually Needed—and When Is ≤200 °C Sufficient?

#### 1.1 Crack-Prone Wrought Aluminium Alloys (2xxx, 6xxx, 7xxx)

The 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx aluminium series are susceptible to solidification (hot) cracking because of their broad freezing ranges—approximately 132 K for Al 2024, 140 K for Al 6061, and 177 K for Al 7075 (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 34-38). Crack-free unmodified AA6061 has been demonstrated at 500 °C powder-bed preheating, yielding modest tensile properties (YS ≈ 60 MPa, UTS ≈ 130 MPa, elongation ≈ 15 %) (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34). For AA7075, a 200 °C base-plate preheat did not eliminate cracking despite producing high relative density (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34). For 2xxx alloys, substrate preheating from 200–400 °C reduced but did not eliminate thermal cracking (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34).

**Grain-refiner alternatives are strongly effective.** Adding 1 wt% Zr nanoparticles to AA6061 and AA7075 powders formed nano-Al₃Zr nucleation sites, promoting equiaxed grain growth and producing crack-free, fully dense microstructures without requiring high preheating (bradfordvialva2021developmentofa pages 45-49). Combining 1 wt% Zr with just 100 °C platform heating significantly reduced porosity and cracking in AA6061 (dixit2022laseradditivemanufacturing pages 16-18). In situ TiAl₃ formation from Ti + B₄C additions produced partial grain refinement and prevented solidification cracks in A6061 (rosito2023processabilityofa6061 pages 1-2). For Al-Cu-Mg alloys, 1.5 wt% Ti reduced average grain size from 6.64 to 1.64 µm and prevented crack formation, while 0.5 wt% nano-CaB₆ reduced cracking in AA2024 (tumulu2025laserpowderbed pages 48-53). Si additions (3–4 wt%) improve Al 7075 processability by promoting eutectic phases and reducing the solidification range (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 34-38). Green-laser processing has also been demonstrated as an alternative, reducing energy density requirements and Mg/Zn evaporation while enabling crack-free 6061 and 7075 with Ti particle additions (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34).

#### 1.2 Al-Mg-Sc/Zr (Scalmalloy®) and AlSi10Mg

Scalmalloy® (Al-4.5Mg-0.73Sc-0.27Zr-0.49Mn) does not require high preheat to prevent cracking; Sc and Zr intrinsically form Al₃(Sc,Zr) nucleants that promote fine equiaxed grains. A 200 °C build platform has been used for in-situ solute clustering and aging during the LPBF process, producing high strength directly in the as-built condition and avoiding a separate heat-treatment step (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2). Conventional peak aging requires temperatures above 300 °C (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2).

AlSi10Mg is the most widely printed aluminium alloy and normally requires no preheat above ambient to 200 °C for crack-free processing. The near-eutectic Si content provides a narrow solidification range, good fluidity, and inherent grain refinement (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34, wang2024areviewon pages 7-9).

#### 1.3 Tool Steels (H13, M2, M50, High-Speed Steels)

For AISI H13 hot-work tool steel (≈0.3–0.4 wt% C), preheating at 200 °C is reported as processible, though results are powder- and parameter-dependent (wu2021hotworktool pages 3-4). Preheating up to 200 °C was associated with compressive stresses, while 300–400 °C produced tensile stresses because the temperature exceeded the martensite-start temperature (platl2021defectsina pages 1-4). For Thermodour 2344 (essentially H13), preheating at 200, 300, and 500 °C was investigated, but cracking was not completely prevented even at 500 °C (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 13-14). The relationship between carbon content, martensite transformation temperature, and cracking is complex—carbon content alone is not a reliable predictor, and thermal conductivity differences between powders can dominate (wu2021hotworktool pages 25-25).

For M2 high-speed steel, cracking occurred at 100 and 180 °C, while 200 °C produced crack-free material in one study (wu2021hotworktool pages 3-4). However, other work found cold cracks persisted across 200–400 °C (bergmueller2022crackfreeinsitu pages 1-2). For M50, substrate preheating up to 500 °C improved processability, with the microstructure changing from epitaxial grain growth at ≈200 °C to columnar dendritic bainitic structure with precipitated carbides at 500 °C (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 12-13). For HS6-5-3-8, approximately 350 °C minimized initial crack formation, but cracks could not be completely avoided even with high-temperature platform preheating (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 12-13). A related grade (HS6-5-8-3) was reported crack-free at 500 °C (wu2021hotworktool pages 3-4). An even higher-carbon steel (1.64 wt% C) required whole powder-bed preheating at approximately 800 °C for crack-free samples (platl2021defectsina pages 1-4).

Crack risk is strongly related to carbon content, with risk initially decreasing over 0.2–0.5% C then increasing. Preheating above the martensite-start temperature suppresses transformation during building but can produce very high residual stress during final cooling (wu2021hotworktool pages 25-25).

#### 1.4 Non-Weldable Nickel Superalloys (CM247LC, IN738LC, IN713LC)

These γ′-strengthened superalloys represent the most demanding case for preheating. For CM247LC and IN713LC, preheating up to approximately 900 °C did not eliminate hot cracking; cracks remained associated with γ′ precipitation and segregation of carbide-forming elements. The study indicated that preheating above the γ′-solvus temperature—exceeding 1200 °C—would be needed to fully suppress cracks (abdelwahed2023crackingmechanismsand pages 1-2). For IN738LC, high-temperature preheating (500–1200 °C) is identified as a key strategy, with crack-free EB-PBF forming demonstrated at 1000 °C using multiple preheating processes (abdelwahed2023crackingmechanismsand pages 1-2). For IN939, 400 °C preheating increased residual stress by 16.2% compared to room temperature, attributed to γ′ precipitation during fabrication (mariana2025innovationsinin939 pages 16-19).

Weldable IN718, by contrast, does not normally require high preheat. Builds at 80, 300, and 500 °C have been investigated, with the main effects being on defect occurrence and stress distribution rather than preventing fundamental cracking (calliariUnknownyearinfluenceofprocess pages 18-22, fassinatoUnknownyearinfluenceofprocess pages 35-40).

#### 1.5 Ti-6Al-4V, TiAl, NiTi, Cu, W, Mo, WC-Co

**Ti-6Al-4V** does not generally require high preheat for crack-free bulk parts; 200–400 °C is used primarily for residual-stress reduction in distortion-sensitive or large builds. The Aeroswift platform targeted 600 °C for large Ti-6Al-4V builds (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3).

**γ-TiAl intermetallics** require whole-build-volume induction heating at approximately 800 °C for crack-free processing (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 3-5).

**Pure tungsten** requires approximately 1000 °C preheating for crack-free processing, though porosity remains an issue (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 13-14).

**WC-17Co** was processed at 900 °C powder-bed preheating on a laboratory-scale Aconity MIDI system, reducing porosity to approximately 2.0 %, though cobalt evaporation, brittle phases (W₂C, η-phase), and delamination remain concerns (fries2020laser‐basedadditivemanufacturing pages 1-2, fries2020laser‐basedadditivemanufacturing pages 3-3).

**Nickel aluminium bronze** (Cu alloy) was investigated from 25–550 °C on an EOS M290-HT, with platform temperature strongly influencing distortion, cracking, and phase formation (saremi2026designingnickelaluminum pages 4-6).

**Molybdenum** printed on AISI 304 stainless steel delaminated after approximately 10 layers due to brittle Sigma phase formation at the diluted interface (≈40–50 wt% Mo). A Cu-OFE plate provided good compatibility (rebesan2021characterizationofmolybdenum pages 70-75).

#### 1.6 Commercial Machines Offering ≥400 °C

**SLM 280**: A commercially available SLM 280 equipped with a preheating system capable of 500 °C has been used for tool steel processing (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 10-11).

**Aconity 3D (MIDI/MINI)**: Known for customized machines with preheating systems above 1000 °C (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 10-11). The AconityMIDI provides a maximum platform temperature of 500 °C, with a build space of approximately 170 mm diameter × 180 mm height, residual oxygen below 100 ppm, and a 200 W single-mode fiber laser (fassinatoUnknownyearinfluenceofprocess pages 35-40). WC-Co was processed at 900 °C on an Aconity MIDI (fries2020laser‐basedadditivemanufacturing pages 1-2). High-speed steel HS2-2-2 was processed on the same platform type at room temperature, 200, 350, and 500 °C under argon with O₂ below 200 ppm (lucke2023influenceoflaser pages 2-5).

**EOS M290-HT**: A modified M290 with a 12.5 cm diameter base plate reaching up to 900 °C. It incorporates VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) modules for upper powder-bed heating up to 1200 °C, with an infrared camera measuring surface temperature every second for dynamic control. Each newly recoated layer can be uniformly heated in less than half a second without separate pre- or post-heating steps. A gas-purification system maintains oxygen below 200 ppm (saremi2026designingnickelaluminum pages 4-6, saremi2026designingnickelaluminum pages 3-4).

**Aeroswift (large-format)**: Uses 3 kW aluminum-nitride ceramic resistive heaters, targeting 600 °C for Ti-6Al-4V. FEA predicted only 395 °C at the heater and 374 °C at the substrate due to multiple conductive heat-loss paths and 44% insulation efficiency. Redesigned concepts predicted 650 °C without additional heater power (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 5-7).

**Induction-heated platforms** have been used for WC-Co at 900 °C and γ-TiAl at 800 °C, and laser-diode in-situ annealing for 316L at 625 °C (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 3-5).

---

### 2. Complications at 400–600 °C

#### 2.1 Powder Flowability, Sintering, and Agglomeration

Particles near the melt pool or exposed to sustained heating can form solid necks or fuse into larger clusters, shifting the particle-size distribution toward coarser sizes and reducing free-flowing, reusable material (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 7-9). These agglomerates can obstruct recoaters or delivery systems, produce streaks or local powder-bed irregularities, and require more energy to melt completely, potentially creating lack-of-fusion defects (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 7-9). Studies on GH3536 Ni-based powder showed that at 100–200 °C the powder remained highly cohesive and non-flowable by Hall flow testing; at 300 °C cohesion decreased enough for some flowability; and at 400 °C the best spreading was achieved (repose angle decreasing from ≈43° at 100 °C to ≈27° at 400 °C) (wang2024effectofparticle pages 7-9, wang2024effectofparticle pages 6-7). However, heating also increased oxygen content to 478 ppm at 400 °C (wang2024effectofparticle pages 7-9). For aluminium powders specifically, the literature identifies moisture, oxide coatings, condensate, and fine particles as the dominant factors controlling cohesion and spreadability, but controlled temperature-dependent flowability data at 400–600 °C for Al LPBF powder is sparse (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 29-30, rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 41-42, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 1-2).

#### 2.2 Oxidation, Mg/Zn Evaporation, and Atmosphere Control

Aluminium powder is hydrophilic and readily forms alumina; humid powder aging increases alumina and hydroxide inclusions and raises oxygen and hydrogen content, destabilizing the melt pool (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 11-12). Over five production cycles, AlSi10Mg powder oxygen content increased by 120 ppm when affected by laser-induced heating, compared with only 10 ppm for powder recycled without heat exposure (sargioti2025physicochemicalandtoxicological pages 2-4). Mg (boiling point ≈1091 °C) and Zn (≈907 °C) are selectively lost from LPBF melt pools at high energy densities; Zn is lost preferentially, with the Zn:Mg ratio decreasing by as much as 33% compared to starting powder at high volumetric energy densities (fields2024structuralandcompositional pages 58-63). These losses reduce the concentrations of strengthening-phase formers (Mg₂Si in 6061, MgZn₂ in 7075) (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 38-42). Metal vapor condenses into nanoscale fume particles (≈10–150 nm) that scatter the laser beam, reduce energy delivery, destabilize melting, increase porosity, and contaminate optics (qin2021influenceoflaser pages 10-12). Excessive gas flow can become turbulent and disturb powder or melt-pool behavior, while insufficient flow allows fume accumulation (qin2021influenceoflaser pages 10-12, qin2021influenceoflaser pages 1-2).

Operating oxygen levels in reported high-temperature systems are generally below 200 ppm (EOS M290-HT) (saremi2026designingnickelaluminum pages 4-6) to below 100 ppm (Aconity MIDI) (fassinatoUnknownyearinfluenceofprocess pages 35-40, lucke2023influenceoflaser pages 2-5). The literature uniformly emphasizes the need for high-purity argon atmosphere and moisture control, but quantitative dew-point specifications for aluminium LPBF are rarely stated explicitly.

#### 2.3 Thermal Management, Distortion, and Part Removal

Preheating can paradoxically increase residual stress in some alloys: for IN939, 400 °C preheating increased distortion by 16.2% (maximum 0.028 mm) compared to room temperature, attributed to γ′ precipitation (mariana2025innovationsinin939 pages 16-19). Very high melt-pool temperatures at elevated preheat can lower melt viscosity, negatively affecting part contour resolution (rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 10-11). The Aeroswift study demonstrated that multiple metal-to-metal contacts and inadequate insulation can prevent the substrate from reaching its target temperature—a ceramic heater design predicted 395 °C at the heater but only 374 °C at the substrate (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 5-7).

Diffusion bonding of parts to the build plate is enhanced at higher temperatures due to reduced thermal gradients and improved metallurgical bonding, making part removal more difficult. Dissimilar material interfaces can form brittle intermetallic phases; Mo on stainless steel delaminated after ≈10 layers due to Sigma phase formation (rebesan2021characterizationofmolybdenum pages 70-75).

---

### 3. Build-Plate Materials, Thermal Expansion, and Plate-to-Bore Fit

#### 3.1 Thermal Expansion Mismatch

For a Ø75 mm 6061 plate at 500 °C in a 316L bore at ≈55 °C, using representative mean CTEs of ≈24–25 µm/m/K for 6061 and ≈16–17 µm/m/K for 316L, the differential diametral growth is approximately 0.36–0.41 mm—substantially more than the ≈0.14 mm stated for the 200 °C tier. This necessitates cold diametral clearances of approximately 0.50–0.65 mm before tolerances, cylindricity, bow, deposits, and seizure margin.

Lower-CTE aluminium plate materials such as 4032 (CTE ≈19 µm/m/K), A390, or other hypereutectic Al-Si alloys would reduce clearance closure. Al-SiC composites offer even lower CTE (≈12–17 µm/m/K depending on SiC fraction) but introduce concerns about reduced ductility, heterogeneous remelting at the first-layer interface, thermal fatigue, and machining difficulty. Spray-formed hypereutectic Al-Si controlled-expansion alloys are commercially available and represent an intermediate option. However, alloy-specific LPBF substrate qualification data for these materials is essentially absent from the peer-reviewed literature.

#### 3.2 Printing Al on Dissimilar Substrates

Dissimilar LPBF interfaces can form brittle intermetallic compounds, crack, or delaminate due to incompatible melting points, thermal conductivities, and CTEs (rebesan2021characterizationofmolybdenum pages 70-75, dubey2024negativethermalexpansion pages 9-11). The formation of brittle intermetallic phases is a primary concern in multi-material LPBF. For aluminium on steel, Fe-Al intermetallics (e.g., FeAl₃, Fe₂Al₅) form at the interface and are notoriously brittle. Aluminium on titanium would similarly form TiAl₃ intermetallics. Aluminium on copper forms Al₂Cu and other phases. These interfaces can compromise adhesion and part removal.

The practical solution is to use alloy-matched sacrificial build plates: aluminium for aluminium builds, steel for steel, Ni-alloy for Ni superalloys, Ti for Ti alloys. Where matching is impractical, a removable interlayer or sheet can be used—for example, a Mo sheet on a stainless platform solved delamination in Mo printing (rebesan2021characterizationofmolybdenum pages 70-75).

#### 3.3 Sealing Between Hot Plate and Cooler Cylinder

Published details of commercial seal designs are extremely limited. The Aeroswift platform used 5 mm Cermex BK2100SW insulation mats between the heater and mechanical components, with Ti-6Al-4V build plates mounted on a mild-steel baseplate inside a stainless-steel 17-4PH powder pool (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 5-7). Elastomeric seals are unsuitable above ≈300 °C.

For 500 °C operation, the literature and engineering practice point to: (1) replaceable compliant graphite felt/foil rings or aluminosilicate ceramic-fibre wipers outside the precision guiding land; (2) stepped labyrinth geometries that limit direct powder migration without requiring a zero-clearance sliding fit; and (3) decoupled guidance and sealing—guide the piston on a cool, long lower land while letting the upper hot plate float radially within its calculated clearance with a compliant upper seal that excludes powder but carries no lateral load (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 19-20, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 5-7).

---

*Table: Literature-supported preheat thresholds and limitations for representative LPBF alloy classes. Values distinguish demonstrated crack-free conditions from temperatures used only for stress, distortion, phase, or in-situ heat-treatment control.*

Unmodified 6061 has been made crack-free at 500 °C, but inoculated alloys can achieve comparable crack control at much lower temperature (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34, dixit2022laseradditivemanufacturing pages 16-18, schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2). |

*Table: Prioritized engineering recommendations for a 500 °C LPBF tier, including thermal architecture, atmosphere, powder handling, substrate selection, sealing, and the plate-to-bore fit.*

---

### Key Conclusions

1. **For the primary aluminium alloy screening mission, 200 °C (Tier A) is sufficient for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and inoculated 6xxx/7xxx/2xxx alloys.** The 500 °C tier is needed primarily for: unmodified 6061 crack elimination, in-situ heat treatment experiments, residual-stress-sensitive thin-wall geometries, and later expansion to tool steels or other crack-prone materials (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34, dixit2022laseradditivemanufacturing pages 16-18, schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2).

2. **Grain-refining additions (Zr, Sc, Ti, TiB₂, TiC, CaB₆) are more effective and far less mechanically complex than a 500 °C platform for eliminating solidification cracking in wrought Al alloys** (bradfordvialva2021developmentofa pages 45-49, tumulu2025laserpowderbed pages 48-53, wang2024areviewon pages 7-9).

3. **The 500 °C tier introduces substantial engineering challenges:** thermal expansion management (≈0.4 mm differential growth for Ø75 mm plate), powder sintering and degradation, accelerated oxidation, Mg/Zn evaporation, insulation inefficiency, component heating, and enhanced part-to-plate bonding.

4. **For tool steels, 200 °C handles H13 and M2 in many process windows; 500 °C extends the range to M50 and some high-speed steels.** Non-weldable Ni superalloys and refractory metals require temperatures far exceeding 500 °C (>900–1200 °C), which are beyond the scope of the proposed Tier B (abdelwahed2023crackingmechanismsand pages 1-2, wu2021hotworktool pages 3-4, rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 13-14).

5. **The EOS M290-HT (VCSEL-based, up to 900 °C base plate, 1200 °C powder-bed top-layer heating) and Aconity MIDI (up to 500 °C standard, >1000 °C customized) represent the current commercial state of the art** for high-temperature LPBF preheating (saremi2026designingnickelaluminum pages 4-6, rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 10-11, fassinatoUnknownyearinfluenceofprocess pages 35-40).

## Build-Plate Preheating in Laser Powder Bed Fusion: When Is 400–600 °C Needed, What Complications Arise, and How Should the Platform Be Designed?

This review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature on high-temperature build-plate preheating for LPBF, covering preheat requirements by alloy class, practical complications, commercial machine implementations, build-plate materials, and plate-to-bore sealing strategies. The findings are organized around the three questions posed, followed by the requested summary table and ranked design recommendations.

---

### 1. When Is 400–600 °C Preheat Actually Needed—and When Is ≤200 °C Sufficient?

#### 1.1 Crack-Prone Wrought Aluminium Alloys (2xxx, 6xxx, 7xxx)

The 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx aluminium series are susceptible to solidification (hot) cracking because of their broad freezing ranges—approximately 132 K for Al 2024, 140 K for Al 6061, and 177 K for Al 7075 (pqac-00000002). Crack-free unmodified AA6061 has been demonstrated at 500 °C powder-bed preheating, yielding modest tensile properties (YS ≈ 60 MPa, UTS ≈ 130 MPa, elongation ≈ 15 %) (pqac-00000000). For AA7075, a 200 °C base-plate preheat did not eliminate cracking despite producing high relative density (pqac-00000000). For 2xxx alloys, substrate preheating from 200–400 °C reduced but did not eliminate thermal cracking (pqac-00000000).

**Grain-refiner alternatives are strongly effective.** Adding 1 wt% Zr nanoparticles to AA6061 and AA7075 powders formed nano-Al₃Zr nucleation sites, promoting equiaxed grain growth and producing crack-free, fully dense microstructures without requiring high preheating (pqac-00000005). Combining 1 wt% Zr with just 100 °C platform heating significantly reduced porosity and cracking in AA6061 (pqac-00000001). In situ TiAl₃ formation from Ti + B₄C additions produced partial grain refinement and prevented solidification cracks in A6061 (pqac-00000004). For Al-Cu-Mg alloys, 1.5 wt% Ti reduced average grain size from 6.64 to 1.64 µm and prevented crack formation, while 0.5 wt% nano-CaB₆ reduced cracking in AA2024 (pqac-00000032). Si additions (3–4 wt%) improve Al 7075 processability by promoting eutectic phases and reducing the solidification range (pqac-00000002). Green-laser processing has also been demonstrated as an alternative, reducing energy density requirements and Mg/Zn evaporation while enabling crack-free 6061 and 7075 with Ti particle additions (pqac-00000000).

#### 1.2 Al-Mg-Sc/Zr (Scalmalloy®) and AlSi10Mg

Scalmalloy® (Al-4.5Mg-0.73Sc-0.27Zr-0.49Mn) does not require high preheat to prevent cracking; Sc and Zr intrinsically form Al₃(Sc,Zr) nucleants that promote fine equiaxed grains. A 200 °C build platform has been used for in-situ solute clustering and aging during the LPBF process, producing high strength directly in the as-built condition and avoiding a separate heat-treatment step (pqac-00000031). Conventional peak aging requires temperatures above 300 °C (pqac-00000031).

AlSi10Mg is the most widely printed aluminium alloy and normally requires no preheat above ambient to 200 °C for crack-free processing. The near-eutectic Si content provides a narrow solidification range, good fluidity, and inherent grain refinement (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000033).

#### 1.3 Tool Steels (H13, M2, M50, High-Speed Steels)

For AISI H13 hot-work tool steel (≈0.3–0.4 wt% C), preheating at 200 °C is reported as processible, though results are powder- and parameter-dependent (pqac-00000007). Preheating up to 200 °C was associated with compressive stresses, while 300–400 °C produced tensile stresses because the temperature exceeded the martensite-start temperature (pqac-00000022). For Thermodour 2344 (essentially H13), preheating at 200, 300, and 500 °C was investigated, but cracking was not completely prevented even at 500 °C (pqac-00000024). The relationship between carbon content, martensite transformation temperature, and cracking is complex—carbon content alone is not a reliable predictor, and thermal conductivity differences between powders can dominate (pqac-00000026).

For M2 high-speed steel, cracking occurred at 100 and 180 °C, while 200 °C produced crack-free material in one study (pqac-00000007). However, other work found cold cracks persisted across 200–400 °C (pqac-00000027). For M50, substrate preheating up to 500 °C improved processability, with the microstructure changing from epitaxial grain growth at ≈200 °C to columnar dendritic bainitic structure with precipitated carbides at 500 °C (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023). For HS6-5-3-8, approximately 350 °C minimized initial crack formation, but cracks could not be completely avoided even with high-temperature platform preheating (pqac-00000023). A related grade (HS6-5-8-3) was reported crack-free at 500 °C (pqac-00000007). An even higher-carbon steel (1.64 wt% C) required whole powder-bed preheating at approximately 800 °C for crack-free samples (pqac-00000022).

Crack risk is strongly related to carbon content, with risk initially decreasing over 0.2–0.5% C then increasing. Preheating above the martensite-start temperature suppresses transformation during building but can produce very high residual stress during final cooling (pqac-00000026).

#### 1.4 Non-Weldable Nickel Superalloys (CM247LC, IN738LC, IN713LC)

These γ′-strengthened superalloys represent the most demanding case for preheating. For CM247LC and IN713LC, preheating up to approximately 900 °C did not eliminate hot cracking; cracks remained associated with γ′ precipitation and segregation of carbide-forming elements. The study indicated that preheating above the γ′-solvus temperature—exceeding 1200 °C—would be needed to fully suppress cracks (pqac-00000006). For IN738LC, high-temperature preheating (500–1200 °C) is identified as a key strategy, with crack-free EB-PBF forming demonstrated at 1000 °C using multiple preheating processes (pqac-00000006). For IN939, 400 °C preheating increased residual stress by 16.2% compared to room temperature, attributed to γ′ precipitation during fabrication (pqac-00000015).

Weldable IN718, by contrast, does not normally require high preheat. Builds at 80, 300, and 500 °C have been investigated, with the main effects being on defect occurrence and stress distribution rather than preventing fundamental cracking (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000044).

#### 1.5 Ti-6Al-4V, TiAl, NiTi, Cu, W, Mo, WC-Co

**Ti-6Al-4V** does not generally require high preheat for crack-free bulk parts; 200–400 °C is used primarily for residual-stress reduction in distortion-sensitive or large builds. The Aeroswift platform targeted 600 °C for large Ti-6Al-4V builds (pqac-00000019).

**γ-TiAl intermetallics** require whole-build-volume induction heating at approximately 800 °C for crack-free processing (pqac-00000046).

**Pure tungsten** requires approximately 1000 °C preheating for crack-free processing, though porosity remains an issue (pqac-00000009).

**WC-17Co** was processed at 900 °C powder-bed preheating on a laboratory-scale Aconity MIDI system, reducing porosity to approximately 2.0 %, though cobalt evaporation, brittle phases (W₂C, η-phase), and delamination remain concerns (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000059).

**Nickel aluminium bronze** (Cu alloy) was investigated from 25–550 °C on an EOS M290-HT, with platform temperature strongly influencing distortion, cracking, and phase formation (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000041).

**Molybdenum** printed on AISI 304 stainless steel delaminated after approximately 10 layers due to brittle Sigma phase formation at the diluted interface (≈40–50 wt% Mo). A Cu-OFE plate provided good compatibility (pqac-00000020).

#### 1.6 Commercial Machines Offering ≥400 °C

**SLM 280**: A commercially available SLM 280 equipped with a preheating system capable of 500 °C has been used for tool steel processing (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000043).

**Aconity 3D (MIDI/MINI)**: Known for customized machines with preheating systems above 1000 °C (pqac-00000043). The AconityMIDI provides a maximum platform temperature of 500 °C, with a build space of approximately 170 mm diameter × 180 mm height, residual oxygen below 100 ppm, and a 200 W single-mode fiber laser (pqac-00000044). WC-Co was processed at 900 °C on an Aconity MIDI (pqac-00000053). High-speed steel HS2-2-2 was processed on the same platform type at room temperature, 200, 350, and 500 °C under argon with O₂ below 200 ppm (pqac-00000057).

**EOS M290-HT**: A modified M290 with a 12.5 cm diameter base plate reaching up to 900 °C. It incorporates VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) modules for upper powder-bed heating up to 1200 °C, with an infrared camera measuring surface temperature every second for dynamic control. Each newly recoated layer can be uniformly heated in less than half a second without separate pre- or post-heating steps. A gas-purification system maintains oxygen below 200 ppm (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042).

**Aeroswift (large-format)**: Uses 3 kW aluminum-nitride ceramic resistive heaters, targeting 600 °C for Ti-6Al-4V. FEA predicted only 395 °C at the heater and 374 °C at the substrate due to multiple conductive heat-loss paths and 44% insulation efficiency. Redesigned concepts predicted 650 °C without additional heater power (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056).

**Induction-heated platforms** have been used for WC-Co at 900 °C and γ-TiAl at 800 °C, and laser-diode in-situ annealing for 316L at 625 °C (pqac-00000046).

---

### 2. Complications at 400–600 °C

#### 2.1 Powder Flowability, Sintering, and Agglomeration

Particles near the melt pool or exposed to sustained heating can form solid necks or fuse into larger clusters, shifting the particle-size distribution toward coarser sizes and reducing free-flowing, reusable material (pqac-00000010). These agglomerates can obstruct recoaters or delivery systems, produce streaks or local powder-bed irregularities, and require more energy to melt completely, potentially creating lack-of-fusion defects (pqac-00000010). Studies on GH3536 Ni-based powder showed that at 100–200 °C the powder remained highly cohesive and non-flowable by Hall flow testing; at 300 °C cohesion decreased enough for some flowability; and at 400 °C the best spreading was achieved (repose angle decreasing from ≈43° at 100 °C to ≈27° at 400 °C) (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). However, heating also increased oxygen content to 478 ppm at 400 °C (pqac-00000047). For aluminium powders specifically, the literature identifies moisture, oxide coatings, condensate, and fine particles as the dominant factors controlling cohesion and spreadability, but controlled temperature-dependent flowability data at 400–600 °C for Al LPBF powder is sparse (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

#### 2.2 Oxidation, Mg/Zn Evaporation, and Atmosphere Control

Aluminium powder is hydrophilic and readily forms alumina; humid powder aging increases alumina and hydroxide inclusions and raises oxygen and hydrogen content, destabilizing the melt pool (pqac-00000035). Over five production cycles, AlSi10Mg powder oxygen content increased by 120 ppm when affected by laser-induced heating, compared with only 10 ppm for powder recycled without heat exposure (pqac-00000037). Mg (boiling point ≈1091 °C) and Zn (≈907 °C) are selectively lost from LPBF melt pools at high energy densities; Zn is lost preferentially, with the Zn:Mg ratio decreasing by as much as 33% compared to starting powder at high volumetric energy densities (pqac-00000034). These losses reduce the concentrations of strengthening-phase formers (Mg₂Si in 6061, MgZn₂ in 7075) (pqac-00000036). Metal vapor condenses into nanoscale fume particles (≈10–150 nm) that scatter the laser beam, reduce energy delivery, destabilize melting, increase porosity, and contaminate optics (pqac-00000038). Excessive gas flow can become turbulent and disturb powder or melt-pool behavior, while insufficient flow allows fume accumulation (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040).

Operating oxygen levels in reported high-temperature systems are generally below 200 ppm (EOS M290-HT) (pqac-00000041) to below 100 ppm (Aconity MIDI) (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000057). The literature uniformly emphasizes the need for high-purity argon atmosphere and moisture control, but quantitative dew-point specifications for aluminium LPBF are rarely stated explicitly.

#### 2.3 Thermal Management, Distortion, and Part Removal

Preheating can paradoxically increase residual stress in some alloys: for IN939, 400 °C preheating increased distortion by 16.2% (maximum 0.028 mm) compared to room temperature, attributed to γ′ precipitation (pqac-00000015). Very high melt-pool temperatures at elevated preheat can lower melt viscosity, negatively affecting part contour resolution (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000043). The Aeroswift study demonstrated that multiple metal-to-metal contacts and inadequate insulation can prevent the substrate from reaching its target temperature—a ceramic heater design predicted 395 °C at the heater but only 374 °C at the substrate (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056).

Diffusion bonding of parts to the build plate is enhanced at higher temperatures due to reduced thermal gradients and improved metallurgical bonding, making part removal more difficult. Dissimilar material interfaces can form brittle intermetallic phases; Mo on stainless steel delaminated after ≈10 layers due to Sigma phase formation (pqac-00000020).

---

### 3. Build-Plate Materials, Thermal Expansion, and Plate-to-Bore Fit

#### 3.1 Thermal Expansion Mismatch

For a Ø75 mm 6061 plate at 500 °C in a 316L bore at ≈55 °C, using representative mean CTEs of ≈24–25 µm/m/K for 6061 and ≈16–17 µm/m/K for 316L, the differential diametral growth is approximately 0.36–0.41 mm—substantially more than the ≈0.14 mm stated for the 200 °C tier. This necessitates cold diametral clearances of approximately 0.50–0.65 mm before tolerances, cylindricity, bow, deposits, and seizure margin.

Lower-CTE aluminium plate materials such as 4032 (CTE ≈19 µm/m/K), A390, or other hypereutectic Al-Si alloys would reduce clearance closure. Al-SiC composites offer even lower CTE (≈12–17 µm/m/K depending on SiC fraction) but introduce concerns about reduced ductility, heterogeneous remelting at the first-layer interface, thermal fatigue, and machining difficulty. Spray-formed hypereutectic Al-Si controlled-expansion alloys are commercially available and represent an intermediate option. However, alloy-specific LPBF substrate qualification data for these materials is essentially absent from the peer-reviewed literature.

#### 3.2 Printing Al on Dissimilar Substrates

Dissimilar LPBF interfaces can form brittle intermetallic compounds, crack, or delaminate due to incompatible melting points, thermal conductivities, and CTEs (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). The formation of brittle intermetallic phases is a primary concern in multi-material LPBF. For aluminium on steel, Fe-Al intermetallics (e.g., FeAl₃, Fe₂Al₅) form at the interface and are notoriously brittle. Aluminium on titanium would similarly form TiAl₃ intermetallics. Aluminium on copper forms Al₂Cu and other phases. These interfaces can compromise adhesion and part removal.

The practical solution is to use alloy-matched sacrificial build plates: aluminium for aluminium builds, steel for steel, Ni-alloy for Ni superalloys, Ti for Ti alloys. Where matching is impractical, a removable interlayer or sheet can be used—for example, a Mo sheet on a stainless platform solved delamination in Mo printing (pqac-00000020).

#### 3.3 Sealing Between Hot Plate and Cooler Cylinder

Published details of commercial seal designs are extremely limited. The Aeroswift platform used 5 mm Cermex BK2100SW insulation mats between the heater and mechanical components, with Ti-6Al-4V build plates mounted on a mild-steel baseplate inside a stainless-steel 17-4PH powder pool (pqac-00000056). Elastomeric seals are unsuitable above ≈300 °C.

For 500 °C operation, the literature and engineering practice point to: (1) replaceable compliant graphite felt/foil rings or aluminosilicate ceramic-fibre wipers outside the precision guiding land; (2) stepped labyrinth geometries that limit direct powder migration without requiring a zero-clearance sliding fit; and (3) decoupled guidance and sealing—guide the piston on a cool, long lower land while letting the upper hot plate float radially within its calculated clearance with a compliant upper seal that excludes powder but carries no lateral load (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000056).

### (b) Ranked Design Recommendations for the 500 °C Tier and Plate Material/Fit

| Rank | Recommendation | Rationale / evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **Do not make 500 °C the default for aluminium screening.** Use Tier A (≤200 °C) for AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and reserve Tier B for unmodified 6xxx experiments, in-situ heat treatment, or exceptionally stress-sensitive geometries. | AlSi10Mg normally prints without high preheat; Scalmalloy uses about 200 °C for in-situ clustering rather than crack prevention. Unmodified 6061 has been made crack-free at 500 °C, but inoculated alloys can achieve comparable crack control at much lower temperature (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031). |
| 2 | **Prefer grain-refining chemistry over a 500 °C plate for 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx development.** Screen Zr/Sc, Ti/TiB₂, TiC, CaB₆, and eutectic-forming additions first. | Zr nanoparticles produced crack-free, fully dense 6061/7075; 1 wt% Zr with 100 °C reduced 6061 cracking; TiAl₃ prevented 6061 cracking; 1.5 wt% Ti prevented cracking in Al-Cu-Mg. By contrast, 200 °C failed for 7075 and 200–400 °C failed to eliminate 2xxx cracking (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000032). |
| 3 | **Replace the 6061 heater block with a mechanically retained steel, precipitation-resistant stainless steel, Ni alloy, or ceramic heater carrier.** Do not structurally load 6061 at 500 °C. | High-temperature platforms require all supporting and moving components to tolerate sustained heat. A ceramic resistive heater can reach the required temperature, but conductive losses through surrounding steel hardware can prevent the plate from reaching its target (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056). |
| 4 | **Thermally isolate the heater assembly from the piston and cylinder.** Use thick low-conductivity ceramic board/fibre insulation, minimized metallic contact area, slender thermal breaks, and radiation shields. | In the Aeroswift study, multiple metal contacts and only 5 mm insulation limited a nominal 600 °C system to much lower plate temperatures; the insulation was only 44% effective. Improved isolation was predicted to permit approximately 650 °C without more heater power (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000056). |
| 5 | **Use a separately water-cooled piston head, seal carrier, actuator interface, and cylinder rim—but interlock cooling flow with heater power.** | Cooling protects bearings, seals, encoder/actuator components, and the honed bore while allowing the removable plate to remain hot. The strong resulting gradient makes clearance and plate bowing critical; commercial high-temperature systems likewise incorporate chamber cooling (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000042). |
| 6 | **Size the cold diametral clearance from the worst differential expansion, not the Tier-A value.** For a Ø75 mm 6061 plate at 500 °C in a 316L bore near 55 °C, differential diametral growth is approximately 0.36–0.41 mm; specify at least about 0.50–0.65 mm cold diametral clearance before adding tolerances, cylindricity, bow, deposits, and seizure margin. | Using representative mean CTEs of approximately 24–25 µm·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for 6061 and 16–17 µm·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for 316L gives about 0.18–0.21 mm **radial** closure—substantially more than the stated 0.14 mm Tier-A closure. The final fit must be validated thermally because a cooled bore and hot plate are non-isothermal. |
| 7 | **Do not use an elastomer as the hot-edge powder seal.** Use a replaceable compliant graphite felt/foil ring or aluminosilicate/other ceramic-fibre wiper outside the precision guiding land; add a stepped labyrinth and powder-catching annulus. | Elastomers are unsuitable around 500 °C, while fibrous high-temperature insulation and graphite tolerate the thermal environment. A labyrinth limits direct powder migration without requiring a zero-clearance sliding fit. Published commercial clearances and proprietary seal geometries are generally unavailable, so qualification testing is required (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000056). |
| 8 | **Decouple guidance from sealing.** Guide the piston on a cool, long lower land or separate bearing; let the upper hot plate float radially within its calculated clearance. | A hot plate tightly guided by the cooler honed bore risks seizure, galling, bore scoring, and plate buckling. The compliant upper seal should exclude powder, not carry lateral load. |
| 9 | **For aluminium builds, retain an aluminium-family sacrificial build plate whenever possible.** Start with 6061/5083 at ≤200 °C; evaluate 4032 or another qualified high-Si wrought/cast plate for Tier B. | Like-on-like aluminium gives predictable remelting, wetting, and removal. Higher-Si aluminium offers lower CTE and better elevated-temperature dimensional stability than 6061, but its LPBF interface, brittleness, flatness, and machinability must be tested. Evidence for specific 4032/A390 LPBF substrate qualification is sparse, so treat this as an engineering trial rather than a literature-proven substitution. |
| 10 | **Use hypereutectic Al-Si or Al-SiC only after coupon-level interface qualification; do not make ceramic-rich Al-SiC the first Tier-B plate.** | Controlled-expansion Al-Si and Al-SiC can reduce clearance closure, but reduced ductility, heterogeneous remelting, ceramic exposure, thermal fatigue, machining difficulty, and uncertain first-layer bonding can outweigh the CTE benefit. Compositionally compatible metallic Al-Si is the lower-risk first trial. |
| 11 | **Avoid direct aluminium deposition on steel or Invar unless a deliberately engineered interlayer/interface is acceptable.** Use a removable aluminium insert clamped to a steel heater carrier instead. | Dissimilar LPBF interfaces can form brittle intermetallics, crack, or delaminate because of incompatible melting points, conductivities, and CTEs. Mo on stainless steel, for example, delaminated after roughly ten layers where a brittle diluted phase formed, demonstrating that substrate compatibility can dominate the build (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| 12 | **Use alloy-matched substrates by material family:** aluminium plate for Al, steel plate for steels, Ni-alloy plate for Ni superalloys, Ti plate for Ti alloys, and compatible Cu/Cu-alloy plate for copper. | Matched plates minimize brittle dilution zones and differential contraction. Where matching is impractical, use a replaceable sheet/interlayer: a retained Mo sheet or Cu-OFE substrate solved an otherwise unsuccessful Mo/stainless interface in published work (pqac-00000020). |
| 13 | **Control oxygen to below 200 ppm at minimum and preferably below 100 ppm before heating; target still lower values for Ti, Mg-rich Al, and long hot soaks. Measure moisture/dew point independently.** | Reported high-temperature systems operate below 200 ppm; Aconity work reports below 100 ppm. Aluminium powder exposed to laser heating gained about 120 ppm oxygen over five cycles versus 10 ppm without heat exposure, and hot spatter is especially oxidation-prone (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000057). |
| 14 | **Bake/purge the empty chamber and hot-zone hardware before admitting production powder, and use only high-temperature-compatible seals, wiring, insulation, and lubricants.** | Heating releases adsorbed water from chamber walls, oxide/hydroxide-bearing powder, insulation, and seals. Moisture thickens aluminium oxide/hydroxide films, impairs spreading and bonding, and supplies hydrogen that can create porosity (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). |
| 15 | **Provide uniform, controllable cross-flow plus an accessible condensate trap upstream of the filter and optics.** Characterize flow at hot operating conditions. | Mg and Zn boil at approximately 1091 and 907 °C and are selectively lost from Al melt pools; condensed metal/oxide particles can be approximately 10–150 nm, scatter the laser, contaminate optics, and accumulate if gas flow is inadequate. Excessive or turbulent flow can disturb powder, so simply increasing flow is not sufficient (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039). |
| 16 | **Thermally shield and, where needed, actively cool the laser window, O₂ sensor sampling line, recoater drive, hopper throat, camera, and chamber lid.** Locate the O₂ sensor in a conditioned bypass rather than directly above the hot bed. | A 500 °C plate radiates strongly into a 6 L chamber; commercial high-temperature systems incorporate chamber cooling and active monitoring. Fume and condensate additionally threaten the window and sensor, while temperature shifts can bias sensors and expand recoater hardware (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042). |
| 17 | **Use a thermally robust recoater and qualify hot spreading with the actual powder.** Prefer a replaceable metal/ceramic blade, force monitoring, and powder with tightly controlled fines; minimize particles below roughly 15 µm for Tier-B trials. | Fines, moisture, oxide coatings, agglomerates, and partial sintering increase cohesion and produce streaks or low-density layers. Agglomerates can obstruct delivery, be dragged by the blade, and create lack-of-fusion defects; heat-affected aluminium condensate further reduces flowability (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). |
| 18 | **Limit and log each powder lot’s cumulative hot exposure.** Initially restrict 500 °C trials to short, shallow builds; segregate hot-zone powder, sieve it, and test oxygen, PSD, flow/spread density, and Mg/Zn composition before reuse. | Thermal exposure produces necking, satellites, agglomeration and oxide/hydroxide condensate. Heat-affected aluminium powder showed much greater oxygen pickup, while agglomerates shift PSD, reduce reusable yield and impair recoating (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000049). |
| 19 | **Design the first layers and removal process for stronger plate bonding at 400–500 °C.** Include sacrificial interface stock, reduced first-layer energy where validated, EDM/bandsaw access, and a plate resurfacing allowance. | Reduced thermal gradients improve bonding and reduce delamination, but also reduce contraction-assisted release and can enlarge the metallurgically mixed interface. Dissimilar interfaces may instead form brittle phases, so mechanical keys or interlayers should be deliberate, not accidental (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| 20 | **Instrument temperature at the plate top, heater, piston head, bore, gas outlet, lid/window and sensor bay; independently trip on overtemperature, lost cooling, low flow, or rising O₂. Consider VCSEL/laser-diode top-layer heating only as a later uniformity upgrade.** | A heater thermocouple can substantially overstate plate temperature: one ceramic-heater design predicted 395 °C at the heater but only 374 °C at the substrate. EOS-type VCSEL heating plus IR feedback can homogenize each recoated layer rapidly, while laser-diode heating has demonstrated in-situ annealing; these methods add optical and control complexity but address the decay of baseplate heating with build height (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046). |


*Table: Prioritized engineering recommendations for a 500 °C LPBF tier, including thermal architecture, atmosphere, powder handling, substrate selection, sealing, and the plate-to-bore fit.*

---

### Key Conclusions

1. **For the primary aluminium alloy screening mission, 200 °C (Tier A) is sufficient for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and inoculated 6xxx/7xxx/2xxx alloys.** The 500 °C tier is needed primarily for: unmodified 6061 crack elimination, in-situ heat treatment experiments, residual-stress-sensitive thin-wall geometries, and later expansion to tool steels or other crack-prone materials (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031).

2. **Grain-refining additions (Zr, Sc, Ti, TiB₂, TiC, CaB₆) are more effective and far less mechanically complex than a 500 °C platform for eliminating solidification cracking in wrought Al alloys** (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

3. **The 500 °C tier introduces substantial engineering challenges:** thermal expansion management (≈0.4 mm differential growth for Ø75 mm plate), powder sintering and degradation, accelerated oxidation, Mg/Zn evaporation, insulation inefficiency, component heating, and enhanced part-to-plate bonding.

4. **For tool steels, 200 °C handles H13 and M2 in many process windows; 500 °C extends the range to M50 and some high-speed steels.** Non-weldable Ni superalloys and refractory metals require temperatures far exceeding 500 °C (>900–1200 °C), which are beyond the scope of the proposed Tier B (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009).

5. **The EOS M290-HT (VCSEL-based, up to 900 °C base plate, 1200 °C powder-bed top-layer heating) and Aconity MIDI (up to 500 °C standard, >1000 °C customized) represent the current commercial state of the art** for high-temperature LPBF preheating (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044).

It also does not identify which temperatures failed, nor does it discuss Zr, Sc, TiB2, or TiC grain refiners as alternatives to preheating. It does provide general context explaining why preheating or other crack-mitigation strategies may be needed: LPBF involves extremely rapid heating and cooling, with cooling rates of 10^4–10^6 K/s, producing substantial residual stresses. This makes alloys with high crack sensitivity and cold-cracking susceptibility difficult to process. The article states that heat treatment is essential for suitable aluminum alloys because it improves mechanical properties and relieves internal LPBF stresses, thereby improving fatigue performance. Aluminum’s low laser absorption, high thermal conductivity, oxide formation, and susceptibility to defects such as residual stress, pores, and cracks further complicate processing. The excerpt notes that AlSi alloys generally have better LPBF formability, but it provides no preheat-temperature comparison or grain-refiner data for the requested alloy groups.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies 500°C bed preheating as sufficient for producing crack-free pure Al6061 by LPBF, with reported tensile yield strength, ultimate strength, and elongation of 60 MPa, 130 MPa, and 15%, respectively. For Al7075, a 200°C base-plate preheat did not eliminate cracking, despite producing samples with high relative density. The text groups 2xxx alloys (including Al2024), 6xxx alloys (including Al6061), and 7xxx alloys (including Al7075) as susceptible to hot cracking. For 2xxx alloys, thermal cracking was reduced by increasing laser power and reducing scanning speed, but cracks persisted even with substrate preheating from 200–400°C; therefore, the excerpt does not establish a successful crack-free temperature for Al2024 or the broader 2xxx family. It also does not provide specific preheat temperatures for all 6xxx or 7xxx alloys beyond the Al6061 and Al7075 examples. Regarding grain refiners, the excerpt gives evidence only for TiB2: increasing TiB2 from 1% to 5% refined AlSi10Mg grains from 6.32 to 1.55 μm, promoted columnar-to-equiaxed transformation, and 2 wt% produced approximately 127 HV microhardness and 444 MPa tensile strength. No information is provided here on Zr, Sc, or TiC alternatives.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report the specific preheat temperatures needed for crack-free LPBF of aluminum 6061, 7075, 2024, 2xxx, 6xxx, or 7xxx alloys, nor does it identify which preheat temperatures failed. It does establish that high-strength wrought Al alloys, including the 2000, 6000, and 7000 series, generally have poor LPBF processability because of wide solidification ranges, poor fluidity, dendritic growth, and high susceptibility to solidification cracking. For A6061, the cited study used an A6061/Ti/B4C powder mixture rather than relying solely on preheating. The intended complete reaction and ceramic reinforcement synthesis did not occur, but TiAl3 formed in situ. This produced partial grain refinement and equiaxed grains, preventing solidification cracks in the optimized samples. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses several complications and effects associated with high-temperature preheating in laser powder bed fusion of metals, particularly around the 400–600 °C range. Commercial PBF-LB/M systems commonly provide preheating up to approximately 500 °C, but such temperatures require machine components—including axes and other moving parts—to withstand sustained elevated-temperature operation. contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports the concern that elevated thermal exposure during LPBF can degrade powder through partial sintering, satelliting, and agglomeration. Particles near the melt pool or exposed to local overheating may form solid necks or fuse into larger clusters. These agglomerates behave as oversized, irregular powder, shifting the particle-size distribution toward coarser sizes and reducing the volume of free-flowing, reusable material. The resulting degradation can impair flow through recoaters or nozzles, disturb powder spreading, and create streaks or local powder-bed irregularities. Agglomerates may also be retained during sieving, causing material loss, or obstruct powder-delivery systems. Because larger clusters require more energy to melt completely, they may produce inclusions or lack-of-fusion defects when standard parameters are optimized for individual particles. The excerpt further associates uncontrolled sintering with reduced flowability, increased porosity, poor surface finish, and dimensional inaccuracies. It notes that thermal exposure can also increase particle surface roughness and alter thermal absorption, potentially contributing to incomplete melting and local lack-of-fusion defects. However, this passage does not specifically quantify the effects of 400–600°C preheating or address oxidation/nitridation of aluminum or titanium, magnesium/zinc evaporation, oxygen-control requirements, diffusion bonding to the build plate, or build-plate thermal distortion.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses several process complications associated with elevated platform temperatures in LPBF of nickel aluminum bronze, particularly in the 400–550 °C range. The heated-platform window was selected using CALPHAD predictions to promote desirable phases while mitigating brittle-phase formation, indicating that high-temperature processing can alter phase stability and increase brittleness if poorly controlled. It does provide relevant context for powder degradation during LPBF. Conventional PBF-LB is described as operating with the powder bed near ambient temperature in an inert environment, which limits further atmospheric oxidation after passive oxide layers form. Consequently, atmospheric oxidation is considered less important than spatter accumulation for reused powder. Spatters can be hot, partly molten particles that are especially prone to oxidation when exposed to oxygen in the build chamber. Their accumulation can alter powder particle-size distribution, morphology, and flowability, and can increase the powder bed’s oxygen concentration. This may promote oxide inclusions in manufactured parts and cause local variations in energy absorption. The excerpt also notes that spatter generation depends on beam energy and size, scan speed, material, and processing-gas purity. Compared with room-temperature preheating, 400 °C preheating increased residual stress, as reflected by a 16.2% increase in distortion, with a maximum measured distortion of 0.028 mm. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide implementation details for the SLM 280 high-temperature option, Aconity MINI MIDI, TRUMPF TruPrint, EOS M290-HT, or Farsoon, nor does it discuss induction, infrared heating, water cooling, or the specific temperatures achieved by those commercial machines. It does, however, describe a relevant large-format LPBF preheating design on the Aeroswift platform. The system was intended to heat the build plates to 600 °C to reduce thermal gradients and tensile residual stress, but testing showed substantially lower performance. Its architecture uses 3 kW aluminum-nitride ceramic heaters, apparently an electrically resistive heating approach, installed in stainless-steel 304 heater holders and separated from them by 5 mm insulation mats. Titanium Ti6Al4V build plates are mounted on a mild-steel baseplate inside a stainless-steel 17-4PH powder pool. The heater holders connect to stainless-steel inner and outer faces, pillars, and a bolted baseplate, creating multiple conductive heat-loss paths. FEA predicted a heater maximum of 395 °C and substrate temperatures of 374 °C; platform testing achieved less than 300 °C above the build plate. The excerpt reports insulation efficiency of 44% and identifies improved insulation and component configuration as the route to higher temperatures, with redesigned concepts predicted to reach 650 °C above the substrate without increasing heater power.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct evidence on LPBF build-plate compatibility, adhesion, dilution, and interfacial failure, although it concerns molybdenum printed on AISI 304 rather than aluminum printed on steel, titanium, or copper. Printing Mo on an AISI 304 plate initially failed because of poor adhesion: delamination began after approximately 10 layers and ultimately caused recoater collision. Interface analysis found that the principal crack originated where Mo dilution was approximately 40–50 wt.%. The diluted Mo–Fe–Cr–Ni region contained brittle Sigma phase, which was identified by XRD and extraction; this phase, together with LPBF residual stresses, was considered a preferential path for crack propagation and brittle fracture. Cracks also followed Mo-enriched regions and occurred near approximately 45 wt.% Mo. In contrast, an oxygen-free electronic copper (Cu OFE/Cu C2) plate showed good compatibility with Mo, and printing remained stable throughout production. A modified AISI 304 platform with grooves, cavities, vacuum retention, and a 2 mm Mo sheet also enabled successful printing while reducing the need for a full Mo build plate. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that preheating reduces cracking in laser powder bed fusion by lowering thermal gradients, but it does not establish a universally crack-free temperature. For a martensitic tool steel, no preheating increased crack tendency, while 120–160 °C only moderately influenced cracking and properties. The lowest preheating condition produced the highest hardness because of higher cooling rates and reduced retained austenite. For high-speed steel M50, substrate preheating up to 500 °C improved processability and reduced cracks. Around 200 °C, epitaxial grain growth was favored; at 500 °C, a columnar dendritic structure and bainitic microstructure with precipitated carbides were promoted, increasing hardness. For HS6-5-3-8, approximately 350 °C minimized initial crack formation, although cracking could not be completely prevented even with high-temperature platform preheating. The excerpt does not specifically discuss H13, direct comparisons among 200 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C for H13, carbon content, Ms temperature, or a definitive crack-free processing window.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the conclusion that preheating affects LPBF cracking through both thermal-gradient reduction and suppression of martensitic transformation. For H13 hot-work tool steel, preheating up to 200 °C was associated with compressive stresses, while 300–400 °C produced tensile stresses because the temperature exceeded the martensite-start temperature. Separate cited work reported reduced crack density in H13 with elevated-temperature preheating, and crack density in X65MoCrWV3-2 was reduced with preheating up to 300 °C. For high-speed steel M3:2 (HS 6-5-3, containing 1.20 wt% carbon), a strong decrease in crack density was observed at 300 °C. The text does not establish that 200, 400, or 500 °C universally produces crack-free parts, nor does it provide direct results for M2, M50, or HS6-5-3-8 specifically. It explains that conventional high-carbon tool steels form hard, low-ductility carbon martensite during rapid cooling, making them susceptible to cracking; preheating above the martensite-start temperature can suppress this transformation. However, the excerpt alone cannot determine an optimum or crack-free temperature at 500 °C.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that Vogelpoth et al. investigated Thermodour 2344 tool steel using preheating temperatures of 200 °C, 300 °C, and 500 °C. Although the higher temperatures exceeded the martensite-start temperature, cracking was not completely prevented. Thus, the passage does not identify 200 °C, 400 °C, or 500 °C as a condition producing definitively crack-free H13/tool-steel parts; it specifically indicates that cracks persisted even at the reported high preheating temperatures. The excerpt does not discuss 400 °C directly, nor does it provide comparative results for high-speed steels M2, M50, or HS6-5-3-8. More generally, it explains that temperatures above conventional platform-heating capability can reduce thermal gradients and surpass critical transformation temperatures early in the build, thereby substantially reducing defect tendency. It also notes that very high-temperature systems may enable processing otherwise difficult materials, but the cited crack-free example concerns elemental tungsten at temperatures up to 1,000 °C, not H13. Porosity remained an issue in such systems. Therefore, the provided passage supports the conclusion that exceeding the martensite-start temperature alone was insufficient to guarantee crack-free Thermodour 2344 parts.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance on how preheating, carbon content, martensite transformation, and thermal conductivity affect cracking during laser powder bed fusion of hot work tool steels. It does not report specific crack-free preheating temperatures for H13, nor does it directly compare 200°C, 400°C, and 500°C. It explains that preheating changes the number of thermally induced transformation events between austenite and martensite, thereby influencing residual stresses and crack formation. At high carbon contents, martensite transformation temperatures can fall below the preheating temperature; when transformation instead occurs during final cooling, the pronounced lattice-parameter change can generate very high residual stress and cracks. Crack risk is strongly related to carbon content, with the cited crack-map critical temperature decreasing over 0.2–0.5% carbon and then increasing. The excerpt also cautions that carbon and transformation temperatures are not the only factors: one medium-carbon powder remained crack-free at room-temperature processing, apparently because its much higher thermal conductivity homogenized temperature more effectively and reduced residual stress. The passage therefore supports investigating preheating relative to Ms and material thermal properties, but it does not provide direct results for M2, M50, HS6-5-3-8, or specific H13 temperature settings.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general evidence that elevated substrate or platform preheating can reduce or prevent cracking in laser powder bed fusion of tool steels. For X65MoCrWV3-2, suitable laser-scanning parameter combinations achieved relative part densities above 99.5% regardless of preheating temperature, but crack formation was reduced or avoided only when elevated substrate temperatures were used. For tool steel 1.2343, high-temperature platform preheating enabled defect-free, crack-free fabrication, with temperatures up to 800 °C also allowing adjustment of the resulting microstructure and hardness. However, the excerpt does not identify the specific preheating temperatures that produce crack-free H13 parts, nor does it compare 200 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C. It also contains no information about M2, M50, or HS6-5-3-8 cracking, carbon content, martensite-transformation cracking, or the relationship between tool-steel preheating and the Ms temperature. Thus, it supports only the general conclusion that elevated preheating is beneficial for crack suppression in some tool steels, not the requested temperature-specific comparisons or metallurgical explanations.

snippets: To reduce the thermal gradient and thus avoid crack formation induced by thermal stresses, substrate plate heating is applied during the LPBF fabrication of various materials.

Several studies have been performed using substrate plate temperatures of 200–400 C on HSS steels with relatively low carbon content, e.g., HSS M2 and the HSS M50, all yielding similar defect patterns, i.e., cold cracks.
Furthermore, substrate plate heating has been demonstrated to reduce crack density, defect frequency, and residual stresses in H13 hot work tool steel.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the conclusion that preheating temperature is a major factor affecting crack formation, microstructure evolution, and phase distribution in hot-work tool steels processed by laser powder bed fusion. It indicates a critical temperature of approximately 170°C for the discussed H13 investigation, but the provided passage is truncated and does not state the complete crack behavior above that threshold. Therefore, it does not directly provide a confirmed comparison of 200°C, 400°C, and 500°C preheating or establish which of those temperatures produces crack-free H13 parts. The excerpt also does not give specific results for M2, M50, or HS6-5-3-8 high-speed steels. More broadly, it cautions against treating carbon content alone as a predictor of cracking: carbon-free maraging powders can still differ in crack behavior, and one powder cracked at all tested preheating temperatures. The likely controlling mechanisms identified here are transformation temperatures and distortion associated with martensitic transformation. Crack morphology can help distinguish fatigue-type cracking from high-bend-loading cracking and thereby identify the relevant material parameters. The passage is relevant to the question’s themes, but insufficient for definitive temperature-by-temperature conclusions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies preheating as a method that can reduce cracking in LPBF of Al-Cu-Mg alloys, particularly when processing at high speeds, but it does not provide a specific heated-build-platform temperature or preheating range. For high-strength aluminum alloys, grain refiners or inoculants such as Sc, Ti, and Zr are reported to disrupt the columnar grain structure and help eliminate grain-boundary cracking while increasing strength. In Al-Cu-based systems, chemical adjustment and Zr addition are also associated with reduced cracking. The excerpt emphasizes that Al-Cu alloys have a large solidification range and are susceptible to hot cracking; Cu contents above approximately 6 wt% are associated with lower crack sensitivity and better weldability, while Mg can deteriorate weldability. Therefore, the cited material supports preheating and grain refinement as complementary crack-mitigation strategies, but it does not establish the preheating temperature needed for Al-Cu alloys containing grain refiners.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the preheating temperatures or in-situ heat-treatment conditions requested for LPBF of Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy), AlSi10Mg, Al-Fe high-temperature aluminum alloys, or Al-Cu alloys. It does, however, explain why thermal and microstructural control is important for Al-Cu alloys: these alloys are susceptible to solidification cracking, particularly when columnar grains develop. The cited mitigation strategy is alloy modification with grain refiners rather than a specified heated-build-platform temperature. For modified Al-9Cu-Mn-Zr, increasing Zr from 0.2 wt% in the cast alloy to 0.9 wt% in the LPBF alloy refined grains and reduced cracking, although excessive Zr may increase the liquidus temperature and produce coarse intermetallic particles. Adding 1.5 wt% Ti to Al-2.25Cu-1.8Mg changed the structure from coarse columnar to fine equiaxed grains, reduced average grain size from 6.64 to 1.64 µm, and prevented crack formation. Nano-CaB₆ additions to AA2024 also refined grains and reduced cracking susceptibility; 0.5 wt% was reported as sufficient. Thus, the passage supports grain-refiner-based crack control but cannot establish the required platform preheating for Al-Cu alloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses evaporative loss of Mg and Zn during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of a 7xxx aluminum alloy. Because Zn and Mg have substantially lower boiling points (907°C and 1091°C) than Al and Cu (2470°C and 2562°C), selective evaporation is expected when the melt pool reaches elevated temperatures. Across the tested process-parameter range, increasing volumetric energy density reduced the concentrations of both elements in the printed material. Zn was lost preferentially relative to Mg, causing the Zn:Mg ratio to decrease by as much as 33% compared with the starting powder. The authors report that energy density, rather than laser power alone, is a useful predictor of elemental evaporation. They model evaporation using vapor pressures and vaporization fluxes through the Langmuir equation, while melt-pool geometry is estimated with the Rosenthal equation; the model and experiments show a strong initial increase in evaporation that levels off at higher energy densities. The excerpt does not provide quantitative data on chamber condensate, fume, soot, or redeposition, nor does it specify required oxygen concentration (ppm O2), oxygen-control limits, or dew-point requirements for LPBF aluminum processing. It also does not report evaporation directly from loose powder separately from melt-pool evaporation.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant information on evaporation and fume formation during LPBF of Zn and, more generally, Zn/Mg alloys, but it does not specifically characterize aluminum alloy powder or melt-pool evaporation. It states that Zn and Mg can undergo massive evaporation losses sufficient to cause substantial compositional changes. Evaporation is promoted by increasing molten-pool temperature and laser energy input; once the vaporization point is exceeded, additional energy produces more evaporation rather than a continued substantial temperature rise, with evaporation carrying excess heat away. Metal vapor cools and condenses into nanoscale evaporation-fume particles, reported here as approximately 10–150 nm in diameter. These particles can scatter the laser beam, reduce the actual energy delivered to the powder bed, destabilize melting, increase porosity, and contaminate or potentially damage chamber optics. Insufficient shielding-gas flow allows residual fume to accumulate, whereas adequate flow removes it and maintains a clean processing atmosphere. Excessively strong flow can become turbulent and disturb powder or melt-pool behavior. The excerpt does not provide quantitative evaporative-loss rates for aluminum, Mg, or Zn, nor does it discuss soot specifically. It also gives no oxygen-concentration or dew-point requirements for LPBF of aluminum alloys; those specifications would need to be obtained from other sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Mg and Zn evaporation as important problems in laser processing of aluminum alloys. Aluminum’s low laser absorption and high reflectivity require relatively high laser power, which can overheat the melt pool and vaporize low-boiling-point Mg and Zn. Reported evaporation rates vary substantially because they depend on laser power, scan speed, atmosphere control, and measurement methods. The text also notes that Mg and Zn losses are common at high energy densities or powder feed rates, although scan speed effects are inconsistent; evaporation is governed by melt-pool temperature, recoil pressure, and vapor-plume dynamics rather than volumetric energy density alone. Aluminum powder oxidation is another key concern: hydrophilic powder readily forms alumina, reducing absorption and causing contamination and poor bonding. Humid powder aging increases alumina and hydroxide inclusions and raises oxygen and hydrogen content, destabilizing the melt pool. Atmosphere and powder-moisture control are therefore essential, particularly because hydrogen can cause gas porosity. However, this excerpt does not provide quantitative condensate, fume, or soot measurements, nor does it specify a required chamber oxygen concentration in ppm or a dew-point limit. It only states that atmosphere control and moisture management affect evaporation, oxidation, and defect formation.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general information relevant to controlling oxygen and moisture during LPBF of aluminum alloys, but it does not discuss Mg or Zn evaporation, evaporative losses from the powder or melt pool, condensate/fume/soot formation, or quantitative oxygen and dew-point specifications. It states that micrometric metal powders are highly susceptible to oxidation because of their large surface area. Gas atomization uses inert gases such as argon or nitrogen to cool the melt and produce spherical powders while avoiding oxygen contamination. Aluminum and titanium alloys have a particularly high affinity for oxygen, increasing oxidation and explosion risks during atomization; consequently, the process atmosphere must be monitored and substantial argon may be consumed. After production, powders are stored in inert-gas-filled bags or vacuum containers to prevent additional oxidation or moisture contamination. The text further notes that oxide layers and moisture affect powder flowability and can contribute to defect formation. Surface oxides may alter laser-radiation absorption and melt-pool melting behavior, and incorporated ceramic oxide material can create internal defects that affect mechanical and fatigue properties. No numerical ppm O2 limit, dew-point requirement, or chamber exhaust/filtration guidance is given.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses evaporative loss of alloying elements during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of aluminum alloys. Because LPBF uses high-energy-density lasers and produces high-temperature melt pools, relatively low-boiling-point elements—including magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), and copper—are susceptible to volatilization. The cited evaporation temperatures are approximately 1090°C for Mg and 907°C for Zn. Loss of these elements can create nonuniform chemical composition and substantially reduce alloy strength and toughness. This is especially important for heat-treatable alloys: Mg contributes to strengthening in 6061, including through formation of the Mg2Si phase, while Mg and Zn form the MgZn2 strengthening phase that is central to 7075 performance. The excerpt does not provide quantitative measurements of Mg/Zn mass loss, vaporization rates, condensate, fume, soot, or chamber contamination during LPBF. It also does not specify required oxygen concentration in ppm, allowable oxygen limits, inert-gas purity, or dew-point requirements for aluminum LPBF. Therefore, the passage supports the general mechanism and metallurgical consequences of Mg/Zn evaporation, but additional process or equipment literature is needed for numerical oxygen and moisture specifications and for characterization of condensed vapor products.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides specific information about the EOS M290-HT heated-platform LPBF system, but does not describe the Aconity MIDI MINI, WC-Co processing at 900°C, SLM 280, TRUMPF TruPrint, or Farsoon systems. The EOS M290-HT is a modified M290 equipped with a high-temperature build platform and a modification unit incorporating process-chamber cooling, inert-gas purification, and process-monitoring capabilities. Its build plate can reach temperatures of up to 900°C. The heating approach uses VCSEL modules together with an infrared camera and dynamic control system. This arrangement allows the uppermost powder-bed layer to be adjusted in less than half a second and held at a constant, homogeneous temperature during laser scanning. The system can uniformly heat each newly recoated powder layer without separate pre- or post-heating steps. VCSEL heating, IR monitoring, and dynamic feedback also provide homogeneous temperature distribution across the powder bed, while process-relevant information such as temperature distribution is recorded for post-build analysis. Thus, the excerpt characterizes EOS’s system as a high-temperature, actively monitored, layer-by-layer powder-bed heating solution, rather than an induction- or resistive-heating platform.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides detailed information about the EOS M290-HT high-temperature LPBF system, but it does not describe the Aconity MIDI MINI, WC-Co processing at 900 °C, the SLM 280, TRUMPF TruPrint, or Farsoon heated-platform systems. The EOS M290-HT has a 12.5 cm diameter base plate and a 23 cm build height, with base-plate temperatures up to 900 °C and an additional upper powder-bed heating and monitoring system reaching up to 1200 °C. VCSEL modules homogenously heat the uppermost powder layer, while an infrared camera measures its surface temperature and records temperature-field data every second. This monitoring is intended to identify and control regions prone to distortion, residual stress, and cracking. The system combines heating, IR monitoring, and dynamic control to maintain temperature uniformity across the powder bed, including for large build heights. A gas-purification system maintains oxygen concentrations below 200 ppm.
